p.seg: As for what is most esteemed by the sages and worthies,
nothing is more esteemed than clarity and wisdom;
(Heaven makes manifest its signs through the three luminaries,
and humans define their measures through clarity and wisdom. )
Of what is precious in clarity and wisdom,
nothing is more precious than discerning people.
(Clarity in calculations and texts
is but one art among the Six Arts;
wisdom in recognizing people
encompasses all official abilities. )
To know people is true wisdom,
thus all talents are correctly ordered,
and manifold undertakings will flourish.
Therefore, when the sage set forth the yáo symbols and images,
he established expressions distinguishing the exemplary from the base.
(The exemplary person is the mentor of the petty man,
the petty man is a resource for the exemplary person;
mentor and resource complete each other,
and this has been true since ancient times. )
When arranging the intent of the Shī poetry,
he then distinguished the elegant and upright practices in customs and mores;
(In the nine regions, the customs differ,
and the ways of the five directions are distinct;
thus the sage establishes teaching without altering localities,
and shapes governance without changing customs. )
When establishing ritual and music,
he then examined the virtue conveyed by the Six Arts and diligent service;
(Though he did not alter the localities,
he always placed poetry and ritual first;
though he did not change the customs,
he always made filial piety and friendship the root. )
When he personally faced south to rule,
he would select outstandingly talented aides and ministers.
All these are intended to promote collective goodness and accomplish Heaven's work.
(To continue Heaven and bring things into being,
the responsibility is extremely weighty.
Therefore, in seeking the worthy and promoting the good,
he always felt as if he never did enough. )
Once Heaven's work is accomplished,
one then receives fame and honor together.
(Loyal ministers exert their utmost and produce results,
the enlightened ruler obtains the worthy and rests easy,
loyalty and affection unite above and below,
from where could slander and calumny arise? )
Thus, Yáo was praised for perfecting illustrious virtues,
Shùn for advancing the sixteen to office;
Tāng was renowned for drawing forth the worthy from Yǒushēn,
Wénwáng was valued for recommending the old man by the Wèi River.
Considering this,
when sages fostered virtue,
who did not labor their clarity and wisdom in seeking people,
and win peace and ease by employing them?
(Selecting talents to feed the cattle,
was how Qín Mùgōng dominated the Xīróng;
relying solely on Zhòng Fù,
was how Qí Huán Gōng accomplished the nine alliances. )
Therefore, though Zhòng Ní remained untried,
and had no one to promote him,
he still classified his disciples into four categories,
and broadly discussed all kinds of talents to distinguish three ranks.
(He placed moral conduct first among the four categories,
and innate understanding above the three ranks;
to be clear in moral conduct opens the gate of principle and righteousness,
to be pure in determination and spirit is the root of talent and wisdom. )
He also praised central harmony to distinguish the virtue of sages,
(The virtue of central harmony—
how utterly complete it is!
Yet so rare in humans for long ages;
Only the sage can truly attain it. )
He valued virtue to encourage the nearly accomplished.
(The son of the Yán clan—
was he not almost perfect?
For three months he did not deviate from benevolence,
thus glimpsed the gate to moral action.
Had he not possessed the lofty nature of a willful man or a benevolent person,
and day by day reached for it,
how could he have carried it through? )
He instructed on the six hindrances to guard against the failings of partial talents.
(The benevolent cherish things,
but their hindrance lies in indecision;
the trustworthy reveal sincerity,
but their hindrance lies in lack of discretion.
Such are the usual failings of partial talents. )
He pondered the wilful and the reserved to understand the talents of the stubborn and the unbending.
(Some advance toward principle and righteousness,
others keep themselves pure and refrain from action.
Those above accommodate both according to their abilities,
and thus both stubbornness and unbending resolve are made use of. )
He deplored impulsive sincerity lacking trustworthiness,
and clarified that apparent wisdom is hard to safeguard.
(A thick appearance hiding deep intentions—
even the sage finds it difficult.
Hear their words and observe their actions,
and then the seemingly trustworthy cannot escape detection. )
He also said: examine what brings them comfort,
observe what they follow,
and thereby know the integrity of their conduct.
(For words, there must be consistency from the beginning to the end;
for actions, one must observe their origin to seek their conclusion,
and thus one may closely discern both outward and inward disposition. )
Such is the meticulousness in recognizing people.
(If such care is not exercised,
official abilities lose their proper order,
and governmental enterprises will fall to ruin. )
Therefore, I dare to follow the sagely teachings,
to record in order the qualities of people,
in the hope of patching what has been lost or neglected.
May widely learned gentlemen review and consider the meaning thereof.
Nine Signs, Chapter One
(People's dispositions and natures,
and aspirations differ.
By observing the spirit and perceiving the appearance,
the forms can be verified in nine ways.)
"Jiǔ Zhēng," Chapter One
Generally, the root of human beings and things
originates from qíngxìng.
(Xìngzhì is received from nature,
while qíng changes due to acquired habits.
Therefore, when observing people and examining things,
one should seek out their xìngzhì. )
The principle of qíngxìng
is most subtle and profound;
without the insight of a shèngrén,
who can fully grasp it?
(Knowledge has no form or appearance;
thus ordinary people cannot behold it,
only the eyes of the shèngrén perceive and illuminate it. )
All those who possess blood and qi
invariably contain the primal unity as their substance;
(if the zhì does not arrive, they cannot endure cold and heat
or pass through the four seasons. )
They receive yīnyáng in establishing their xìng;
(since xìng is based on yīnyáng,
the meanings of firmness and gentleness are thereby distinguished. )
They embody the wǔxíng and manifest form.
(Bones are strong and sinews are supple,
both deriving their essence from jīn and mù. )
If there is form and zhì,
it can still be directly sought.
(Since qì is outwardly revealed in color,
the physiognomist can discern the fundamental qíng. )
For all people, the quality of their nature,
central harmony is the most precious.
(When the quality is pure, it receives color;
when the flavor is sweet, it receives harmony.
Central harmony
is the root of all conduct,
and the good field of human feelings. )
The quality of central harmony
must be plain and tasteless;
(precisely because it is plain,
therefore the five flavors can be harmonized by it.
If it is bitter,
then it cannot be sweet;
if it is sour,
then it cannot be salty. )
Thus it can regulate and complete the five materials,
transforming and responding in accordance with the times.
(Plain and without bias,
all materials must be governed by it,
uses will be appropriate,
change and communication will not be obstructed. )
Therefore, in observing people and examining their qualities,
one must first look for their plainness,
and only afterwards seek their intelligence.
(Take for example a jìlù horse:
although it surpasses and stands above others,
if its temperament is not harmonious,
it will surely encounter the disaster of breaking its bit, smashing its head, or tearing its chest. )
Intelligence
is the essence of yīn and yáng.
(With separated eyes, lowered ears,
thus arise seeing and hearing. )
When yīn and yáng are clear and harmonious,
then there is wisdom within and brightness without.
The sage is pure and radiant,
able to possess both excellences.
He knows the subtle and the evident,
(his ears and eyes observe together,
he penetrates the hidden and understands the subtle,
appoints abilities according to their office,
and in his selections there is nothing omitted. )
If not a sage,
none can attain both.
(Though something may be obtained through the eyes,
it is perhaps lost to the ears. )
Thus an明 bái scholar,
grasps the mechanism of movement,
but is dim in mysterious reflection;
(skilled in advancing and moving forward,
but dim in stopping and being still.
If he relies on this to advance,
he desires speed and brings on harm;
if he applies it to deep thought,
he resists and seizes but cannot enter. )
One who is profound in reflection,
understands the source of stillness,
but is hindered in quick response.
(His nature is peaceful and silent,
but his wisdom is lacking in timely response.
If he applies this to tranquility,
then the way of profundity and subtlety is achieved;
but if he uses it to aid the world,
he may be strong and swift yet achieve nothing. )
Just as fire and sun emit external light,
but cannot illuminate within;
metal and water reflect within,
but cannot shine outward.
(Each person has their ability,
each thing its own nature.
Therefore, the sage employs clarity and insight to advance,
entrusts the accomplishment of steadfastness to mysterious reflection,
and only then are movement and stillness kept in measure,
going out and remaining at home are in accord with appropriateness. )
The meaning of these two,
is in fact the distinction of yīn and yáng.
(Yáng is active and yīn is still,
this is the fixed nature of Heaven and Earth,
how much more so for people and things? )
If one measures their material qualities,
and examines them in relation to the five substances,
the signs of the five substances
are each manifest in their bodies.
(Bamboo-like courage is green in color,
blood courage is red in color,
the movement is internal, the form external,
how could it be concealed? )
In their bodies,
there are wooden bones, metal tendons, fire qi, earth flesh, and water blood—
these are images of the five substances.
(The five natures
are the tools that shape the form.
The five substances are the mother,
therefore the qi and color follow them and are complete. )
In the reality of the five substances,
each has what it provides.
The five natures differ,
each has that which it receives by endowment,
and when one nature is abundant, then partiality arises.
Thus, when bone is upright yet pliant,
it is called hóngyì;
hóngyì
is the substance of rén.
Wood provides shade downward,
and is the substance of rén.
If the substance is not hóngyì,
rén cannot be completed.
When qi is pure and radiant,
it is called wénlǐ;
wénlǐ
is the root of lǐ.
Fire gives illumination,
and is the root of lǐ.
If the root lacks wénlǐ,
lǐ cannot be completed.
When the body is upright and solid,
it is called zhēngù;
zhēngù
is the foundation of xìn.
Earth must produce life,
and is the foundation of xìn.
If the foundation is not zhēngù,
xìn cannot be completed.
When the sinews are strong and refined,
it is called yǒnggǎn;
yǒnggǎn
is the determination of yì.
Metal can sever and cut,
and is the determination of yì.
Without yǒnggǎn,
yì cannot be completed.
When the color is even and unimpeded,
it is called tōngwēi;
tōngwēi
is the source of zhì.
Water flows freely and reaches everywhere,
and is the source of zhì.
If the source lacks tōngwēi,
zhì cannot be completed.
The five substances have constant natures,
therefore they are called the wǔcháng.
The five substances
are the constant qi of Heaven and Earth;
the five virtues
are the constant conduct of living beings.
The distinctions among the Five Constants,
categorized as the Five Virtues, are as follows:
Thus, warmth, uprightness, flexibility, and firmness
constitute the virtue of wood;
warmth without uprightness leads to weakness,
and flexibility without firmness leads to loss of resolve.
Hardness, constraint, magnanimity, and determination
constitute the virtue of metal;
hardness without constraint leads to rupture,
and magnanimity without determination leads to deficiency.
Willingness, respectfulness, order, and reverence
constitute the virtue of water;
willingness without respectfulness leads to rebellion,
and order without reverence leads to chaos.
Broad-mindedness, awe, gentleness, and uprightness
constitute the virtue of earth;
broad-mindedness without awe leads to laxity,
and gentleness without uprightness leads to dissolution.
Simplicity, ease, clarity, and penetration
constitute the virtue of fire.
Simplicity without ease leads to stagnation,
and clarity without penetration leads to obscurity.
Though the forms undergo infinite transformation,
they still depend on the five natures.
Human emotions and dispositions are manifold and ever-changing,
impossible to exhaust and measure.
Yet tracing them to their source,
they are always rooted in the Five.
Therefore, the signs of hardness and softness, clarity and ease, steadfastness and solidity
manifest in appearance and form,
are revealed in voice and color,
express themselves in emotions and flavors,
each according to its image.
Such is the principle of nature,
the spirit moving from form and color.
When sincerity arises within,
virtue radiates brightly outward.
Thus, when one’s mind and nature are clear and upright,
their bearing is strong and steadfast;
when the mind and nature are tranquil and decisive,
their bearing is advancing and vigorous;
when the mind and nature are balanced and orderly,
their bearing is peaceful and at ease.
Indeed, bearing in motion forms deportment,
each with its own manner:
the movement of upright bearing
is firm and resolute;
the movement of tranquil bearing
is diligent and steady;
the movement of virtuous bearing
is dignified and elevated.
As for the movement and comportment of one’s appearance,
they arise from the qì of the heart.
The qì of the heart is within;
the appearance is manifested outwardly.
The evidence of the qì of the heart
is thus seen in changes of the voice.
When the heart is not unified,
then the concord of the voice is altered.
Indeed, qì joined together forms sound;
sound responds to lǜ and lǚ:
that which is clear and bright is lǜ,
that which is harmonious and level is lǚ.
There is the sound of peace and harmony,
the sound of clarity and ease,
and the sound of modulation and return.
The qì of the heart differs,
thus the sound that is produced is likewise different.
When sound flows smoothly with qì,
it truly contains appearance and color:
without qì, sound cannot be formed,
but once sound is formed, appearance responds in turn.
Therefore, when one is truly rén,
there must be an expression of gentleness and warmth;
when one is truly yǒng,
there must be an expression of dignity and intensity;
when one is truly zhì,
there must be an expression of clarity and insight.
Since voices vary in their pipes,
so too does the appearance vary in form.
That the appearance is manifest in the countenance
is called the evidence of spirit.
The pace, whether slow or fast, of the facial expression
serves as evidence of the spirit.
The evidence of spirit appears in the countenance,
thus emotions are manifested in the eyes.
The eyes are the emblems of the heart,
thus they respond to the heart in their expression.
Thus for rén,
the vital essence of the eyes
is sincere and upright;
when the heart is not leaning or unstable,
the gaze does not turn or deviate.
For yǒng,
the vital essence of the gallbladder
is resplendent and strong.
When the resolve is not timid or cowardly,
the gaze does not wither or falter.
Yet all these are abilities which reach only to one extreme,
and are qualities founded on overcoming.
Not yet can one be awe-inspiring without severity,
nor stern without anger.
Therefore, if the quality of overcoming is not refined,
then affairs do not reach their conclusion.
Able in courage but not in caution,
every action is inevitably followed by regret or blame.
Thus, being upright but not gentle brings woodenness;
wooden strength seeks confrontation,
thereby losing true uprightness.
Being forceful but not refined brings only brute strength;
one may lift cauldrons or run legless,
yet lose proper vigor.
Being firm but not upright brings foolishness;
clinging stubbornly to oneself, thinking oneself right,
one falls into dull stupidity.
Having qì without clarity results in heedlessness;
one’s speech is not clear or smooth,
and in raving nothing is accomplished.
Being fluent but not balanced results in dissolution.
One who delights endlessly in wisdom
is dissipated and loses all bounds.
Therefore, a nature attuned to the mean
is different from these sorts.
One who is brave yet able to be cautious,
benevolent yet able to decide,
whose constitution embraces both,
is thus the chief among all characters.
The five virtues fully equipped,
all encompassed in calmness without flavor.
When one has internalized the measure of salt and sour,
one uses flavorlessness as the guide.
The five qualities are internally abundant,
the five essences are externally manifest.
When the five qualities are calm and settled,
pure radiance makes the exterior splendid.
Thus the eyes manifest the light of the fivefold brilliance.
When the heart is clear, the eyes are bright;
they shine of themselves.
Thus it is said, “When things are born, they have form;
forms possess shén and essence.”
Regardless of worthiness or foolishness,
all receive their endowment of qì and constitution, the nature of yīn and yáng;
only wisdom differs in subtlety or coarseness,
and form differs in depth or shallowness.
By seeking the essence of their color,
and observing their deportment,
down to menial slaves and herdsmen,
all may be ascertained in this way.
One who can know spirit and essence
can exhaust principle and fulfill nature.
The sage thus observes the activities of the world and analogizes them in form and countenance,
and therefore can exhaust principle and fulfill nature, attaining destiny.
The utmost of xìng’s nature
is the manifestation of the nine qualities.
Yīn and yáng generate each other,
and their numbers do not exceed nine.
Thus, the changes in nature and emotion,
their qualities are likewise alike.
Thus, the evenness or unevenness of quality lies in shén,
and shén
is the master of quality.
Therefore, when shén is even, quality is even;
when shén is uneven, quality is uneven.
Brightness or dimness in reality resides in jīng;
and jīng
is the root of reality.
Thus, when jīng is clear, reality is bright;
when jīng is turbid, reality is dim.
The momentum of courage or cowardice lies in qì;
and qì
is the function of momentum.
Therefore, when qì is strong, the momentum is courageous;
when qì is weak, the momentum is cowardly.
Firmness or weakness of support is in gǔ;
and gǔ
is the foundation of support.
Therefore, when gǔ is hard, support is firm;
when gǔ is soft, support is weak.
The decision between restlessness and calm lies in qì;
and qì
is the place of decision.
When qì thrives, the decision is restless;
when qì is harmonious, the decision is calm.
The feeling of sorrow or joy lies in sè;
and sè
is the sign of emotion.
Therefore, a withered countenance comes from sorrowful feeling;
a pleasant countenance comes from joyful feeling.
The decline or uprightness of form lies in yí;
and yí
is the outward expression of form.
Therefore, when yí declines, it is because the form is endangered;
when yí is upright, it is because the form is dignified.
Movement of attitude is seen in róng;
and róng
is the symbol of movement.
Therefore, when movement deviates, so does bearing;
when movement is upright, so is bearing.
The state of slowness or urgency lies in speech.
Speech
is the manifestation of the heart.
Therefore, when the heart is tolerant, speech is slow;
when the heart is narrow, speech is urgent.
As a person,
if their qualities are plain and even,
wise within and bright without,
with strong qì and firm support,
clear voice and joyful countenance,
exalted in yí and upright in bearing,
then all nine qualities are fully present—
this is the virtue that is pure and refined.
If not a person of utmost virtue,
who could match this?
If there is deviation among the nine qualities,
that deviation becomes perversity,
and thus one’s talent is partial and mixed.
Some might have a clear voice and joyful countenance,
yet lack evenness and calmness in quality;
or strong qì and firm support,
yet not be exalted or upright in yí.
With three degrees unlike,
their virtue is named differently.
Those with partial talent bear the name of a single utmost;
those with combined talent hold the title of virtue and yí;
those with combined virtue embody the norm of zhōngyōng.
Therefore, those of partial utmost
name themselves by their talent;
just as all artisans and many skills
each have their own names.
Those of combined talent
take virtue as their designation;
of rén, yì, lǐ, zhì,
they take one as their title.
Those of combined virtue
are given still finer names.
The Dào cannot be explained by a single aspect,
nor virtue handled from a single side.
That which nurtures all things is not called rén;
that which equalizes all forms is not called virtue.
Calmly even and undifferentiated,
without boundary with things,
who can know its name?
Therefore, when combined virtue reaches the utmost,
it is called zhōngyōng;
dwelling in the center and walking in constancy,
thus it is called zhōngyōng.
Zhōngyōng
is the designation of the sage.
Great rén cannot be approached,
great yì cannot be repaid;
to be called so without virtue,
is to place one’s name in that of the sage.
Specific and subtle,
this is called déxíng;
and déxíng
is the title of the great refined.
Practicing rén to draw close to things,
establishing yì to benefit rén,
achieving virtue through losing Dào—
this is but a secondary path.
To reach one utmost is called partial talent;
partial talent
is the quality of the small refined.
Only rén without yì,
only yì without rén—
unable to be all-encompassing,
each holds to one practice;
thus their name does not reach the great refined.
A single quality is called resemblance;
resemblance
is a category of corrupted virtue.
Pure bluntness seems upright but is not upright;
pure abandonment seems open but is not open.
A single utmost with a single deviation is called mixed;
mixed
is the man without constancy.
When good and evil are intermixed,
the heart is undecided.
With no constancy of conduct,
how can one be measured or deliberated?
Those without constancy, and the merely resembling,
are both the end drift of the folk.
Those whose hearts are particularly hard
are those unreached by teaching and transformation.
As for the qualities of the final drift,
they cannot all be discussed,
so they are mostly omitted and not generally treated.
Yet they multiply into crowds,
how could they be counted!
Distinctions of Form, Chapter Two
Endowment receives qì of yīn and yáng,
and nature possesses firmness and gentleness.
Constraint opposes refinement and substance,
and the forms differ from each other.
Section Two: Distinctions of Form
As for the virtue of zhōngyōng,
its essence has no name.
Vast and not confined to a single form,
no one can describe it.
Thus, salty yet not brackish—
if you call it xián,
there is no brackishness to accommodate,
as Gōngchéng’s hundred brines are all the same as saltiness.
Bland yet not insipid—
if you call it bland,
its taste is still not insipid.
Substantial yet not coarse—
if you call it substantial,
its pattern is not simply unadorned.
Refined yet not gaudy—
if you call it refined,
its brilliance is not painted in colors.
It can be awe-inspiring and embrace,
it can be discerning and reserved,
dwelling in the harmony of saltiness and blandness,
standing between substance and refinement.
Therefore, from a distance it appears solemn,
but as you approach, it is refined;
its words fill the world with no waste.
Its transformations have no fixed pattern,
yet it takes achievement as its measure.
It responds to change and fits transformation,
all to achieve thorough understanding of things.
Therefore, those who are aggressive surpass it,
exerting themselves vigorously on the path of striving forward.
But those who are constrained fall short;
settled and inactive outside the bounds of aggression and restraint.
When one is rigid or defiant by nature,
thus he will demonstrate clear excellence,
but also suffer certain losses in principle.
If one excessively nurtures the physical form,
then tigers devour them from without;
if one dwells in lofty halls with thin walls,
then illness attacks from within.
Therefore, harsh rectitude and firm resolve—
their value lies in correcting the crooked,
but their fault lies in being quarrelsome and contentious;
assaults and accusations arise from harsh firmness.
Gentleness, compliance, and easy forgiveness—
these are found in tolerance and leniency,
but their fault is lack of decisiveness;
excessive suspicion arises from timidity and forgiveness.
Bravery and heroic strength—
they rely on courageous daring,
but their fault is in jealousy;
lawlessness is born of fierceness and defiance.
Excellence and prudent caution—
their virtue is in humility and respectfulness,
but their fault is in excessive doubt;
difficulty and suspicion originate in excessive caution.
Sturdy firmness and strong resolve—
their usefulness lies in being reliable and steadfast,
but their fault is in stubborn inflexibility;
self-centeredness comes from obstinacy.
Argument and discerning reasoning—
their strength is in resolving entanglements,
but their fault is in drifting and dissipation;
arrogance and carelessness arise from clever debate.
Broad knowledge and universal understanding—
their greatness is in being generous and inclusive,
but their fault is in mixing with impurity;
muddiness originates from over-broadness.
Purity, uprightness, honesty, and cleanliness—
their discipline is in frugality and firmness,
but their fault is in being petty and confined;
narrowness comes from excessive integrity.
Noble motion and openheartedness—
their accomplishment lies in aspiring and climbing upwards,
but their fault is in being scattered and excessive;
carelessness arises from being too forthright.
Composure and deep secrecy—
their refinement is in subtle and mysterious depth,
but their fault is in slowness;
sluggishness arises from too much stillness.
Simplicity, openness, and utter directness—
their quality is in sound honesty,
but their fault is in lack of subtlety;
carelessness comes from too much directness.
Much wisdom and concealed feelings—
their advantage is in cunning strategy,
but their fault is in excessive ambiguity.
Hidden deviation comes from suppressed feelings.
When one constantly advances in virtue,
weighing the mean to restrain the rigidity and obstinacy of one’s talents,
the defiant one acts on his own judgment to strive forward,
the stubborn one acts on his own judgment to guard his boundaries.
And by pointing out the faults of others to intensify their shortcomings,
the rigid become more rigid,
the defiant become more defiant.
Some sink with burdens like stones,
some clutch wood and perish in blazing fire.
Just like the sword-bearing men of Jìn and Chǔ,
continually deceiving and contradicting each other.
From the perspective of Jìn looking at Chǔ,
they laugh that Chǔ is on the left;
from Chǔ looking at Jìn,
they laugh that Jìn is on the right.
Though left and right differ,
each employs his own usage,
but those who fail to understand principle
slander and revile each other without cause.
Rigidity and defiance oppose each other,
in all cases it is just like this.
Therefore, a forceful and resolute person,
harsh, rigid, and lacking in harmony,
does not beware of the aggressiveness of his strength,
and regards compliance as weakness,
strengthening his resistance.
To consider gentleness and compliance as feebleness,
and to elevate the aggressive spirit in his heart.
Therefore, he can establish laws,
but is difficult to engage in subtlety.
If one is harsh, forceful, rigid, and unyielding,
how can the workings of subtlety find entry?
A gentle and compliant person,
slow of heart and broad in judgment,
does not guard against negligence in attending to affairs,
and regards resistance as wounding,
settling into comfort.
To view forceful resistance as harmful injury,
and to content the heart with forgiveness and patience.
Therefore, one can follow established norms with him,
but it is difficult to deal with him in matters of weighing uncertainty.
If one is slow of heart and indecisive,
how can he weigh matters of doubt?
A valorous and fierce person,
with spirit roused and courage decisive,
does not beware lest his bravery be his downfall,
and considers compliance as cowardice,
exhausting his strength.
To regard patient compliance as timidity,
and thus exhaust the energy that leads to his own ruin.
Therefore, he can be relied on to face difficulties,
but is unsuited to dwell in constraint.
With fierceness and self-destructive impulse,
how can he abide restriction?
A fearful and cautious person,
frightened of trouble and full of suspicion,
does not beware lest his timidity impede righteousness,
and takes courage as presumptuousness,
increasing his doubt.
To view boldness and forthrightness as frivolous insult,
and to augment the doubting and fearful disposition.
Therefore, he can help preserve and sustain,
but finds it hard to stand by principles.
If one is fearful of trouble and full of suspicion,
how can he establish principles and righteousness?
A person with the demeanor of Líng Kǎi,
holds fast to powerful will and unique character,
does not beware lest feelings become stubborn and overprotective,
and regards discernment as deceit,
thus reinforcing his exclusivity.
Considering broad discernment to be empty and insubstantial,
and thus strengthening his mind's single-mindedness.
Therefore, he can uphold integrity,
but is difficult to harmonize with the multitude.
With steadfast will and persistence,
how can he win the attachment of the many?
A person broad in discernment,
eloquent in argument and resourceful in reasoning,
does not beware lest his words become excessive and overflowing,
and sees uprightness as constraint,
letting his current flow.
To view uprightness and correctness as restriction and impediment,
thus pursuing an unrestrained and wandering heart.
Therefore, he can be used to order things broadly,
but is hard to establish boundaries with.
If one is rich in discernment and his words overflow,
how can any substantial limits be made firm?
A magnanimous and universal person,
affectionate in will and harmoniously accommodating,
does not beware lest his associations become muddled and mixed,
and sees integrity as narrowness,
thus expanding his murkiness.
To consider steadfastness as narrow rigidity,
and enlarge his heart’s tendency to disorder and mixture.
Therefore, one can use him to soothe the masses,
but it is hard to make customs strict with him.
When all is mingled and harmonized without discrimination,
how can one enforce social customs?
A person who is upright and uncompromising,
acts as a corrective,
(pinyin: fǔ lián fǎn),
clear and sharp against impurity,
does not beware lest his way become narrow and confined,
and considers universalism as defilement,
thus increasing his restraint.
To see broad inclusiveness as contaminated and impure,
thus furthering the restricted nature of his own heart.
Therefore, he may be used to uphold integrity,
but has difficulty in adapting and transforming.
Where the way is confined and the fords are narrow,
how can one traverse the open way?
A person at ease in movement,
has ambitions set on transcendence,
does not beware lest his intentions become excessive and reckless,
and considers stillness to be stagnation,
thus sharpening his edge.
To treat deep calm as dull restraint,
and to encourage a keener and more forceful spirit.
Therefore, he is fit for progress and advancement,
but finds it hard to hold back or follow behind.
With intent set on surpassing,
how can humility and restraint be maintained?
A person who is calm and tranquil,
his thoughts travel in winding turns,
does not beware lest his stillness causes excessive delay,
and regards action as carelessness,
esteeming meekness.
To view agitation as crude neglect,
and to prize timidity within his own mind.
Therefore, he is suited to deep and subtle consideration,
but is not apt for swift action.
If thoughts turn in winding reflection,
how can one attain quick responses?
A simple and open person,
inner doubts yet externally sincere,
does not beware lest his factuality be rustic and blunt,
and sees cunning as fantasy,
revealing his honesty.
To view expediency and artifice as flimsy deception,
and so reveal his own faithfulness and sincerity.
Therefore, he is suitable for establishing trust,
but not for exchanging signals.
If reality is genuine but blunt and rustic,
how can matters of lightness and gravity be properly weighed?
A person skilled in concealing and cunning,
fundamentally measures and accommodates,
does not beware lest his methods depart from uprightness,
and takes utter devotion as foolishness,
valuing emptiness.
To see honest completeness as simpleminded directness,
thus exalting hollowness and insubstantiality in his own mind.
Therefore, he may be praised for his skill,
but finds it difficult to rectify deviation.
Where cunning and art depart from the right path,
how can error and deviation be corrected?
Learning
is what enables one to become accomplished;
fortitude and resolve strengthen one’s firmness,
gentleness and compliance discipline one’s weakness.
Forbearance
is what allows one to extend empathy;
by extending one’s own feelings,
one understands the natures of things.
The nature of a partial talent cannot be altered.
If one stubbornly clings to one’s own nature
and, hearing what is right, does not change,
then even if taught through learning,
talent may be developed but will be lost accordingly.
If a nature of fortitude has already formed,
the heart seeking conflict becomes ever more resolute.
Even if instructed through forbearance,
emotional extension will each follow its own inclination.
That which the will considers wrong,
one will not agree to in others.
The trusting person, contrary to trust,
extends his own trust
and believes all people are trustworthy,
so the deceitful find room to practice falsehood.
The deceitful person, contrary to deceit,
extends his own deceit
and believes all people are deceitful;
thus the trustworthy may fall under suspicion.
Therefore, if learning does not attain the Way,
if forbearance does not reach all things,
those of partial talent
each believe only in their own ability—
how can the Way penetrate them,
or things be reached in their entirety?
This is the great loss from partial talent.
If talent cannot encompass all,
further instruction only increases the loss.
Therefore, the ruler of things employs the rén of others to remove their greed,
employs their wisdom to remove their deceit,
and only then are all talents brought under mastery,
and the Way can reach all things.
Flowing Endeavors, Section Three
The Three Materials are the source,
those who practice are the flow.
As the flow gradually loses the source,
their endeavors each become different.
"Transmitted Karma," Chapter Three
Generally, among the pursuits of humankind,
there are twelve in all.
Since natures are not the same,
and habits and practices differ,
the branches and currents diverge,
each possessing its own pursuit.
There are the families of pure integrity,
whose conduct serves as a model for others.
There are the Fǎjiā,
who establish laws and set regulations.
There are the Shùjiā,
whose resourcefulness knows no bound.
There are those of national structure,
possessing the three qualities in full measure.
There are those of skill and ability,
possessing the three qualities to a lesser degree.
There are judges of worth,
who distinguish right from wrong.
There are artisans,
adept and ingenious in their crafts.
There are the wise and thoughtful,
able to unravel many doubts.
There are those of literary talent,
skilled in composing prose and analogies.
There are those learned in Rúxué,
thoroughly discerning the Way and its arts.
There are eloquent speakers,
quick and ready in response.
There are the heroes and outstanding figures.
Their courage and strategy surpass others.
As for those whose virtue and conduct are lofty and exquisite,
whose bearing and demeanor serve as models,
these are called the houses of pure integrity;
Yán Líng and Yàn Yīng are such.
Those who establish laws and institutions,
strengthen the state and enrich the people,
are known as the Fǎjiā;
Guǎn Zhòng and Shāng Yāng are such.
Those who comprehend the Way and transformation,
whose strategies and schemes are marvelous,
are known as the Shùjiā;
Fàn Lǐ and Zhāng Liáng are such.
Those who possess all three talents,
with all three talents complete,
virtue and law,
and techniques all in perfect measure—
their virtue is sufficient to inspire customs,
their law is sufficient to rectify the world,
their techniques are sufficient to achieve victory in the ancestral temple;
these constitute the body of the state,
Yī Yǐn and Lǚ Wàng are such.
Those who possess all three talents,
yet whose three talents are each slight,
and not purely complete,
whose virtue is enough to lead a single state,
whose law is enough to rectify township and village,
whose techniques are enough to weigh matters appropriately,
these are called competent functionaries;
Zǐ Chǎn and Xīmén Bào are such.
Those who possess a distinction among the three talents,
each belonging to a single stream.
The three talents are the source,
while those who study and practice become the streams.
Among those of the stream of pure integrity,
if they cannot be generous and forgiving,
and take purity as principle,
how can they be lenient?
They are fond of reproach and censure,
discriminating between right and wrong;
if they do not forgive others,
then disputes arise.
This is called judgment and criticism;
the followers of Zǐ Xià are such.
Those of the stream of Fǎjiā,
if they cannot originate far-reaching plans,
focus their laws and institutions on what is near,
and their thoughts do not reach what is distant.
Yet they can fulfill the duties of an official,
apply intent and craft skilfully,
with their efforts fixed on achieving success,
thus clever ideas arise.
This is called workmanship and skill;
Zhāng Chǎng and Zhào Guǎnghàn are such.
Those of the stream of Shùjiā,
if they cannot originate and establish enduring models,
pursue achievement with techniques,
so they do not leave lasting models.
Yet they adapt in times of change and use expedients,
their cunning and wisdom abundant,
but public rectitude insufficient,
those long on expediency,
must be short on uprightness.
This is called cunning insight;
Chén Píng and Hán Ānguó are such.
All these eight professions,
are based on the three talents.
Without virtue, law cannot be properly guided;
without law, techniques cannot flourish.
Thus in the establishment of these eight professions,
the three talents are always the basis.
Therefore, though the streams may flow and be distinguished,
all are materials for managing affairs.
Just as ears and eyes have their separate functions,
yet their use achieves the same result;
though the talents of the group differ,
their achievements are unified.
Those who are able to compose literature and write,
are called writers;
Sīmǎ Qiān and Bān Gù are such.
Those who can transmit the work of the sages,
but cannot manage affairs or implement governance,
are called Confucian scholars;
Máo Gōng and Guàn Gōng are such.
Those whose eloquence does not attain the Way,
yet who respond resourcefully in conversation,
are called debaters;
Yuè Yì and Cáo Qiūshēng are such.
Those with courage and strength surpassing the masses,
whose abilities and strategies exceed others,
are called heroes of prowess;
Bái Qǐ and Hán Xìn are such.
All these twelve talents,
are the responsibilities of ministers;
each upholds their own talent,
but cannot possess them all,
and safeguard a single office,
thus are the responsibilities of ministers.
The ruler's virtue is not involved therein.
The ruler’s virtue is
to be intelligent and even-tempered,
able to understand and embrace all types of talent,
yet not personally taking charge of affairs.
He does not seek to see through his own eyes,
nor does he personally listen with his own ears;
each official performs his own duty,
and thus all the various talents are utilized.
When all talents have been put to use,
the ruler may sit with folded hands, do nothing, yet still govern effectively.
Therefore, when the Way of rulership is established,
then the twelve kinds of talent each attain their proper post.
If the one above takes no action,
then those below take up their responsibilities.
The virtue of integrity and restraint
is the duty of the Shīshì;
he is in charge of morals and virtue,
teaching the noble descendants the Way.
The talent of Legalists
is the duty of the Sīkǒu;
he administers laws and statutes,
to prohibit and restrict villainy and violence.
The talent of Strategists
is the duty of the Sāngū;
he manages temple planning,
assisting in fair public deliberation.
When the three types of talents are purely provided,
they become the responsibility of the Sāngōng;
their rank is among the Three Scholars,
who sit and discuss the Way.
If the three talents are minor,
it is the duty of the Zhǒngzǎi;
as minister of Heaven’s offices,
he commands all the officials.
The talent of judgment and criticism
is the aide of the Shīshì;
distinguishing right from wrong,
thereby assisting the Shīshì.
The talent of wisdom and meaning
is the aide of the Zhǒngzǎi;
he guides and adjusts systems as needed,
thereby assisting the minister of Heaven’s offices.
Artisan talent
is the duty of the Sīkōng;
applying intent and skill,
thus he oversees the Winter Offices.
The scholar’s talent
is for settling the people;
he manages by virtue and perseverance
to secure the safety of the people.
The literary talent
is charged with the dynastic history;
he compiles constitutions and records events,
passing them on to future generations.
The talent of eloquence
belongs to the Xíngrén;
he manages responses,
escorting and receiving along the roads.
The talent of the bold and heroic
is the duty of generals and commanders;
they manage army and force,
quelling rebellions and the disobedient.
This is called when the ruler’s Way is achieved and the ministers’ order established,
officials do not trade responsibilities,
thus peace and prosperity are accomplished.
The reason great peace is achieved
is because officials and people do not shift their duties.
If the feet try to grab things,
the hands try to walk,
how could the four limbs find peace?
How then could the Way of governance be orderly?
If the Way is not even and impartial,
and uses only one skill to please,
it is like a great carpenter skilled with the compass,
yet only using the compass.
Thus, if one talent holds the balance,
the rest lose their proper functions.
Only use the compass,
then the square cannot establish its right angles,
the line cannot be stretched straight;
though one uses ruler and square by day,
nothing can be accomplished.
Talents and principles, Chapter Four
Since talents follow divergent paths,
principles also have different courses.
Thus, when discussing the various talents,
only then are the principles determined.
“Cáilǐ,” Section Four
To establish affairs and set forth principles,
nothing can be determined without order.
If words are settled beforehand, there is no confusion;
if affairs are settled beforehand, there is no stumbling.
But when it comes to debate and disputation,
few are able to decide matters.
What is the reason for this?
It is because principles are manifold, and human talents differ.
Affairs are myriad in their aspects,
and human emotions are confused and mixed;
who can decide them?
When principles are manifold, they are hard to grasp;
when talents differ, motives become strange.
Strange motives and difficulty in understanding—
then principles are lost and affairs deviate.
With strange motives and many principles,
how can one attain the desired end?
Principles have four divisions:
Dào, Yì, Shì, and Qíng,
each with its own category.
Clarity has four schools,
each school thoroughly grasping the four divisions,
each with its own lineage.
Emotions have nine deviations;
when emotion offends clarity,
there are nine possible gains and losses.
Drift has seven semblances,
seeming right but actually wrong,
and their kinds are sevenfold.
Explanation has three failures;
when one's words dominate but the principle is stagnant,
the failures are three in number.
Debate has six provocations;
forcefully contending for superiority and competing in spirit,
the provocations are sixfold out of anger.
Comprehension has eight abilities.
Keen hearing, acuity of thought, clarity of understanding, and penetration,
these are the eight abilities by which one comprehends.
As for the transformations of Qì by Heaven and Earth,
fullness and emptiness, decrease and increase,
these are the principles of Dào;
transforming people by means of Dào
adapts with the changing times.
Laws, methods, and the proper conduct of affairs,
these are the principles of matters;
governing people by law
relies on constitutional institutions.
The rites and teachings should be appropriately suited,
these are the principles of righteousness;
instructing with reason
allows for proper advancement and withdrawal.
The pivots of human emotions,
these are the principles of feeling.
Observing the true state of things
lies in words and speech.
The four principles are different;
as for their relation to talent,
clarity and distinction are required.
Clarity is manifested through substance in practice.
Therefore, when substance aligns with principle,
this alignment brings about clarity;
when there is enough clarity, principle becomes evident;
when principle suffices, a tradition is established.
Dào yì and actual affairs each form their own school.
Thus, when one's disposition is plain and even,
the mind is subtle and profound,
demeanor is neither hasty nor disturbed,
and the heart is careful and thorough,
one can reach naturalness—
such is the household of Dàolǐ;
taking Dào as principle,
one is thus able to reach naturalness.
If one's disposition is alert and penetrating,
resourceful and quick-witted in strategy,
demeanor never sluggish,
then the mind is quick and sharp.
Able to manage complexity swiftly,
this is the household of affairs and principle;
taking affairs as principle,
one thus judges complexity well.
If one's disposition is harmonious and moderate,
able to discuss ritual and propriety,
demeanor never inappropriate,
then ritual and propriety are attained in balance.
Able to discern gain and loss,
this is the household of righteousness and principle;
taking righteousness as principle,
thus one is clear about gain and loss.
If one's disposition is resourceful and perceptive,
able to deduce feelings and original intent,
demeanor never acts recklessly,
then the essence of things is well understood.
Able to adapt to change,
this is the household of emotion and principle.
Taking emotion as principle,
thus one can fully explore the transformations of things.
The clarity of the four schools being already distinct,
there exist nine partialities of sentiment.
When sentiment infringes upon clarity,
each has its own gains and losses.
Clarity arises from authenticity,
sentiment is stirred by nature.
If sentiment prevails over clarity, then there is obscuration,
so even if something is gained, it will inevitably be lost.
People of gānglüè disposition,
cannot manage subtleties.
Their intentions are coarse and negligent,
their thoughts lack profundity and subtlety.
Therefore, when discussing the grand scheme,
they are expansive and lofty;
a firm disposition brings distant ambition.
When traversing fine details,
they wander unanchored and are careless and estranged.
Far-reaching ambition thus leads to estrangement.
People of kànglì character,
cannot bend or yield.
Their intentions are fierce and forceful,
their ambition does not turn or bow.
When discussing law or principle directly,
they are encompassing and impartial;
a severe temperament produces resolute judgment.
When speaking of adaptation and change,
they are obstinate and do not assimilate.
Firm reasoning becomes stagnant and hindered.
People who are jiānjìng,
delight in attacking concrete matters.
Their intentions are upright and exact,
their words are not vacuous or hesitant.
When indicating mechanisms and principles,
they are bright and penetrating to the utmost;
with certainty in character, their words are exhaustive.
When treading the great doctrine,
they are direct and exposed, holding to it alone.
If their words are incisive, the meaning is slight.
People who are biànjí,
speak copiously and with sharp intent.
Their thoughts are swift and urgent,
their ambition does not countenance withdrawal or setback.
When deducing human affairs,
they are perceptive and reach the limits of reasoning;
a sharp temperament seeks the utmost in reason.
When it comes to great righteousness,
they are broad but startled and not comprehensive.
Focusing on fine reason overlooks the great.
People who are fúchén,
cannot think deeply.
Their intentions are vacuous and expansive,
their ambition is not profound or subtle.
In arranging order and number,
they are open-minded and arrogantly knowledgeable;
a floating nature leads to proud ambition.
When establishing essential matters,
they are flashy and unsettled.
Pride in ambition makes the rationale sparse.
Those who are shallow in comprehension,
cannot tackle deep difficulties.
Their intention is shallow and gentle,
their thinking is not deep or mature.
When listening to argument and debate,
they are quick to draw analogies and are easily pleased;
a shallow temperament makes for easy pleasure.
When scrutinizing subtle principles,
they turn about and lack foundation.
Easy pleasure leads to lack of foundation.
People who are kuānshù,
cannot be nimble and swift.
Their intentions are slow and unhurried,
their thoughts are not rapid or urgent.
In discussing rényì,
they are expansive and detailed, genteel and elegant;
a forgiving temperament makes for refined judgment.
When pursuing current affairs,
they are slow and cannot keep up.
Gentility and leisure result in slowness.
People who are wēnróu,
do not have inexhaustible strength.
Their intentions are warm and moist,
their ambition is not for beauty or joy.
When tasting the Dao and reason,
they are compliant and harmonious;
a harmonious nature yields smooth reasoning.
When meeting doubt and difficulty,
they are soft and indecisive.
Smooth reasoning thus wavers between affirmation and denial.
Those fond of the strange,
are unrestrained and seek the extraordinary.
Their intentions are unusual,
their ambitions do not conform with others.
In creating expedient schemes,
they are unconventional and splendidly bold;
a strange temperament values magnificence.
When examining clear doctrine,
they are eccentric and circuitous.
Strangeness and aloofness bring expansiveness and oddity.
This is what is meant by the nine partialities of sentiment,
each follows what the heart considers reasonable.
What the heart takes as reasonable,
right and wrong obscure each other,
never coming to an end.
If one’s nature is not pure and free-flowing,
then there are seven kinds of seeming in discourse:
There are those who talk at length and set forth old arguments,
appearing as if they are well-versed in current matters;
whose words are superficial and flow with elegance,
seeming as if suitable for adoption.
Some offer little reasoning yet many points,
resembling those of broad understanding;
their phrases are verbose, their analogies far-reaching,
seeming as if profound and wide-ranging.
Some refute views yet fit the intent,
appearing to clarify and praise;
outwardly pretending approval,
but inwardly lack comprehension.
Some speak last and uphold the long view,
following where the many are comfortable,
seeming able to listen and judge;
yet in truth without knowledge themselves,
as if remaining silent.
They observe the talk of the group,
praising what pleases the majority.
Some dodge difficulties and do not respond,
seeming as if possessing surplus understanding,
but in reality do not know;
truly unable to discern,
they feign forgetfulness and do not answer,
as if knowing but withholding a reply.
Some admire being adept and eloquent,
seeming pleased but not truly joyful;
upon hearing words, at once they expound,
resembling those who explain well,
yet their hearts are vague and cannot comprehend.
Some, due to emotional excitement, lose their way,
and when at an impasse, claim subtlety;
though their words are exhausted,
they think themselves profound, yet have not exhausted the subject.
If they stumble, they snatch at scraps and fragments,
their reasoning already in disarray,
yet they stubbornly force connections.
In truth, they seek two explanations,
seeming like logic that cannot be subdued.
Words fail, logic falters,
their mind delights in having two explanations,
but they continue to speak nonetheless,
and the listeners think they have not been refuted.
All these seven kinds of seeming,
are what perplex most people.
Without a bright mirror, who can discern them?
As for argumentation, when reason prevails,
reason, being ultimate, cannot be moved.
There is also victory by rhetoric.
When rhetoric is skillful, it cannot be forced into submission.
He who triumphs by reason
properly distinguishes black and white to broaden his discourse,
elucidates subtleties and makes them understood;
he explains matters clearly,
as if applying powder and rouge.
He makes bright distinctions,
and his rhetoric is not jumbled or confused.
He who triumphs by rhetoric
breaks right reason to seek what is different;
but if he seeks difference, rectitude is lost.
Using arguments such as “a white horse is not a horse,”
he may win over a thousand people in a single morning.
Yet when confronted with gatekeepers and prohibitions,
he goes straight ahead and only then errs.
Now, among the talents of the nine partialities,
some are alike,
some are opposed,
some are mixed.
When alike, they resolve each other,
like water flowing into water.
When opposed, they refute each other,
like fire being extinguished by water.
When mixed, they broaden each other.
It is not necessary then to be entirely alike,
nor is difference required;
thus, broad comprehension is achieved.
Therefore, one who is skilled in joining discussions
considers the strengths at hand and debates accordingly.
Using what the other can do,
his words are easily understood.
If after repeated attempts no movement results,
then one should not persist;
if the opponent’s thoughts are fixed on dogs,
then horses must wait for another day.
If there is no keen listener nearby,
then debate is not difficult.
In every case of mutual debate,
one speaks for those who understand.
He who is not skilled in joining discussions
argues with confused and opposing points,
while the other’s thoughts are on dogs,
he speaks of horses;
while the other is focused on great similarities,
he addresses minor differences.
When he argues in a confused and opposing manner,
his words do not penetrate.
Trying to fit the square into the round,
reason can never be satisfied.
He who is good at giving analogies
clarifies many matters with a single phrase.
When rhetoric adheres to reason,
few words are needed and the point is clear.
He who is not good at giving analogies
cannot make one idea clear with a hundred words.
When rhetoric deviates far from reason,
even with a flood of words,
one does not make himself clear,
so how much less could others understand?
If with a hundred words he does not clarify a single idea,
he is not worth listening to.
If he does not himself grasp the meaning,
who will listen to him?
This is the threefold failure of discourse.
Those skilled in disputation
make it their task to clarify the root of the matter.
They always stop upon obtaining the principle.
Those unskilled in disputation
abandon the root and attend to the branches.
They pursue the other’s words and respond accordingly.
To abandon the root and attend to the branches,
then the argument becomes contrived.
Failing to seek the root principle,
but instead adorning with troublesome words.
Those skilled in attacking the strong
first subdue their opponent’s vigor and sharpness;
when encountering an adversary who is strong and forceful,
at the start, their spirit is sure to be high.
Therefore, those skilled in attacking the strong
avoid their first onslaught.
They support the main intent,
and gradually press their attack.
By the third round of exchanges, their spirit wanes,
and when it declines, the attack becomes easy.
Those unskilled in attacking the strong
seize upon the opponent’s slip of the tongue,
to blunt their sharp intention;
when the strong have keen intent,
their words may err momentarily,
striking at mistakes to blunt their edge—
this is the challenge of argument.
If one blunts the opponent’s keen intent,
then conflict is stirred.
It is not only a matter of clashing words among the group,
but may even lead to agitated voice and countenance.
Those skilled in pursuing the opponent’s faults
point out where they have stumbled.
If the other has made a misstep,
a brief indication suffices without pressing them.
Those unskilled in pursuing faults
use the other’s concession to attack their nature.
They seize on their stumbles to oppress and wound them.
By using their concession to attack their nature,
then resentment is fostered.
It is not only a matter of tone and look,
but resentment and enmity grow in the heart.
Sometimes what one constantly contemplates and seeks
is only attained after a long time.
When urgently trying to explain to someone,
if they do not quickly understand,
it is deemed difficult to explain.
Having thought upon it long oneself, one is not forgiving toward others.
Deeming it difficult to explain,
then anger is stirred.
It is not only resentment,
but contentious anger arises.
When dispute is at its height,
errors in argument are hard to avoid.
When emotions are strong and words err,
one should rather avoid it.
Those skilled in disputation
bring their opponents back to reason.
When emotion is subdued and intentions return,
they come to mutual accord.
Those unskilled in disputation
overwhelm and provoke the other;
even wishing to show consideration,
there is no way to do so.
When one disregards the other’s mistakes and attempts to show consideration,
but does not heed their words,
with no way to reconcile,
then wild contention arises.
Speaking recklessly without criticism,
they let words run at random.
Whenever people have something on their mind,
their ears cannot hear.
When their thoughts are present,
even thunderclaps are unheard.
Thus, when each thinks and speaks at once,
they strive to restrain one another,
each wishing the other to listen to themselves.
Stopping the other’s words
is to make them hear oneself.
But the other, being preoccupied with their own thoughts,
does not fully grasp one’s meaning,
and so it is deemed that they do not understand.
But it is not lack of understanding;
when one speaks,
because the other’s thoughts are elsewhere,
the listener does not comprehend.
People invariably conceal their lack of understanding.
If told they do not understand,
their nature is to conceal and grow angry.
In concealing their lack of understanding,
anger is stirred.
Then, amid rage and wrath, they no longer heed right or wrong.
All these six sources
are origins from which conflict arises.
Yet although there may be changes and disruptions,
there is still something to be gained.
In creating affairs and establishing principles,
one must have order and reason settled first.
Thus even if there are changing interpretations over small matters,
ultimately it comes to reason being settled and achievement established.
If discussions are not made difficult,
and each presents his own views,
then none will know the proper source.
If everyone contends in argument,
and questions are not made hard to answer,
then none will know which can be used.
From this we may say,
those who discuss and yet settle reason
are truly rare.
Principles are manifold,
human feelings differ.
Therefore, utterances fill the court,
and none is willing to bear the blame.
One must have keen hearing to follow the sequence,
ascend heights to compose,
seek things and give them names,
like Yán Huí listening to weeping,
or Cāng Shū measuring elephants.
One must have thought to create a beginning,
like Zǐ Zhǎn plotting to invade Jìn,
thereby winning the alliance of the feudal lords.
One must have clarity to perceive the opportunity,
like Yú Pián noticing a movement of the eye,
at once knowing that the Qín army was retreating.
One must have eloquence to discern intent,
like Yī Jí replying to the King of Wú,
saying, “One bow, one rise,
is not enough to be called toilsome.”
One must have agility to correct losses,
like Guō Huái replying to the Emperor of Wèi,
saying, “I know I will certainly escape the penalty of Fāngfēng.”
One must have perseverance to await attack,
like Mòzǐ telling the people of Chǔ,
“My disciples already await them at Sòng.”
One must be able to attack and seize the defended,
like Máo Suì advancing,
saying, “Today I follow Chǔ,
not Zhào.”
The King of Chǔ accordingly thanked him.
One must be able to take and easily give.
With your spear,
exchange for the other’s shield,
and then the owner’s argument is exhausted.
Having all these eight qualities,
only then can one fully penetrate the principles of the world.
Penetrating the principles of the world,
one can understand people.
If one cannot possess all eight excellences,
but has but one ability,
such a person is called one of partial talent.
What he can attain is partial,
and what he possesses will differ in appearance.
Each uses what he has mastered,
and establishes his name thereby.
Therefore, keen hearing able to follow sequences
is called the talent for naming things;
thought able to create beginnings
is called the talent for construction;
clarity able to perceive opportunities
is called the talent for comprehensive perception;
eloquence able to discern intent
is called the talent for clear expression;
agility able to correct losses
is called the talent for quick adjustment;
perseverance able to await attack
is called the talent for upholding argument;
attack able to seize the defended
is called the talent for thorough analysis;
being able to take and easily give
is called the talent for trading arguments.
A person of comprehensive talent,
once possessing these eight talents,
practices them in accordance with the Way.
When speaking with a knowledgeable person,
they understand together and minds are enlightened to each other;
being in agreement, they affirm each other,
and thus minds are mutually understood.
When speaking with the general multitude,
one observes their expressions and follows their dispositions.
When below there is arrogance,
one avoids their shortcomings.
Even if one understands all principles,
one does not exalt oneself over others;
always holding to humility,
thus one is able to stand above things.
Clever and resourceful,
yet not putting oneself before others.
Always embracing withdrawal and humility,
thus coming before things.
When speaking well, one expresses oneself,
and stops when the principle is fulfilled.
When the principle is understood, one stops,
not seeking to trouble with excess words.
Mistakes lie with people,
but one does not press them for their faults.
Upon seeing others stumble in error,
one at once steers clear.
Express what others hold in their hearts,
and support what others can do.
In supporting and assisting what others can do,
then everyone takes up their own responsibility.
Do not transgress others’ taboos by using similar situations,
for what reason would you incur resentment?
When speaking with a blind person,
do not shun mention of blindness and such matters.
Do not use your own strengths as the standard for others.
If you have martial power,
do not associate with the likes of roaring tigers.
In argument, state straightforwardly or change as needed,
fearing nothing hateful.
One of broad talents judges matters equitably,
establishes trust before remonstrating,
and even if touching the dragon’s scales,
causes no harm to anything.
He selects the good tones in the chirping of insects,
not discarding their fine melodies because of their ugly sound.
He praises the chance finds of the foolish,
not dismissing their excellent words because of their ignorance.
To take and give as appropriate,
to go and stay without attachment.
When others are at their height of pride,
to humble oneself fully, not being stingy;
not avoiding sharp setbacks,
not begrudging to bend and yield.
When conquering difficulties,
be victorious without boasting.
Let reason conquer,
what is there to be proud of?
When the heart is calm and the will enlightened,
with neither favoritism nor bias,
entrust right and wrong to reason,
and do not covet victory to seek fame.
Strive only to attain the Way.
Such a one can discourse on governing the world and managing affairs.
Broad and carefree, harboring no preconceptions,
entrusting everything to what is utterly appropriate.
Thus, the business of the world will be self-managed,
and all things be self-regulated.
Talents and Abilities, Chapter Five
Talents and abilities differ in size and measure;
their standards are not the same.
Assign tasks according to one's capacity,
and the appointed duties will thus be accomplished.
“Talents and Abilities,” Chapter Five
Someone said:
Among people of talent, there are those who are capable of great things yet incapable of small things,
just as a cauldron that can hold an ox cannot be used to cook a chicken.
In my humble view, this does not define true expertise.
A person of talent is like a vessel:
their size differs.
Some liken a large cauldron that cannot cook a chicken
to a person of great talent who cannot manage small matters,
but this misses the true meaning.
For the term “capable”
arises from a defined designation.
First there is a fixed substance,
and only then does the name “capable” appear.
How could someone be capable in great things but not in small ones?
Whenever people speak of being capable in the great but not in the small,
such words arise from differences in character, some broad-minded, some urgent.
Those who are broad-minded are magnanimous,
while those who are urgent are hasty.
There are such differences in temperament,
and thus it is fitting that there are great and small.
The broad-minded and magnanimous are suited to govern large matters,
while the hasty and urgent are fit to manage small ones.
A person of magnanimity
is suited to administer a jùn or guó,
allowing subordinates to exercise their abilities,
while overseeing their achievements as a whole;
the hasty will become entangled in minutiae,
and no affair will succeed.
A person who is urgent in small matters
is suited to manage a district of one hundred lǐ,
so affairs can be handled by themselves.
A magnanimous person will let the net have holes,
and all matters will be neglected.
Thus, a jùn and a xiàn
are simply large and small versions of different entities.
If one is able to govern a large jùn,
then one can govern a small jùn;
if able to govern a large xiàn,
then also able to govern a small xiàn.
If we distinguish using true understanding of temperament,
then we should speak of different appropriateness for large and small,
not of being capable of the great but not of the small.
If one were capable of the great but not the small,
would Zhòngní not have served as minister to Jì-shì?
As for the chicken and the ox,
they are also simply examples of big and small forms,
if a cauldron can cook an ox,
then it can also cook a chicken;
if a pot can cook a chicken,
it cannot cook a calf.
Therefore, cauldrons, too, should come in various sizes.
If you use it to cook a calf,
how could it not be able to cook a chicken?
There is only what is appropriate or inappropriate,
not what is possible or impossible.
Therefore, if one can govern a large jùn,
then also can govern a small jùn.
Pushing this argument further,
each person of talent is suited to different roles,
not merely a matter of large and small.
The civil official manages the hundred offices,
the military official leads the army.
Indeed, people of talent differ,
each has their own strengths:
some possess the talent of self-responsibility,
cultivating themselves and maintaining personal integrity,
while commanding all officials;
some have the ability to establish laws for others to follow,
with laws displayed and people fearing them,
so that no one dares to violate them;
some have the ability to deliberate and defend,
their intelligence and judgments precise,
acting with proper discretion in all situations;
some possess the virtue to instruct others,
whose teachings are deeply understood,
and whose every action serves as a lesson for others;
some excel in managing affairs so that others accept remonstrance,
reasoning aptly,
their conduct fitting each occasion;
some are skilled in investigation and criticism,
supervising right and wrong,
making distinctions in all things;
some possess extraordinary ingenuity,
using unconventional strategies,
to accomplish tasks and win merit;
some have power and bravery.
Their valor is well-known,
and their might shakes enemy states.
When one can arise from talent,
and talent varies in measure,
since the gifts differ,
their charge in government is likewise distinct.
Thus, one who relies on his capability
is of the integrity and purity type.
Therefore, in the court,
it is the role of Zhǒngzǎi,
and as to governing the state, it is upright and correct administration.
His conduct is proper,
so he presides over the Tiānguān and oversees the myriad heads.
One who is able to establish law
is a person of the Fǎjiā type.
Therefore, in the court,
it is the role of Sīkòu,
and for the state, governance is impartial and just.
The law shows no partiality,
hence he manages the Qiūguān and prosecutes the wicked and violent.
The ability for planning and strategy
is the gift of the Shùjiā type.
Thus, in the court,
it is the duty of the Sāngū,
and for the state, rule is adaptive and transformative.
He is discerning in calculation and deliberation,
thus he assists the Sānhuái and helps in deliberating on the Dao.
The skill in managing human affairs
is the ability of the Zhìyì type.
Therefore, in the court,
he is assistant to the Zhǒngzǎi,
and for the state, governance is harmonious and well integrated.
With keen insight and intent,
he aids the Tiānguān to harmonize internal and external matters.
The ability to put things in practice
is the talent of deference and yielding.
Therefore, in the court,
he is assistant to the Sīkòu,
and for the state, governance is supervision and accountability.
Handling the multitude of affairs,
he assists the Qiūguān in overseeing arrogance and insolence.
The skill in extraordinary means
is the talent of crafts and techniques.
Therefore, in the court,
it is the role of Sīkōng,
and for the state, administration is over the arts and crafts.
Adept in skills and techniques,
he is charged with the Dōngguān and brings the crafts to completion.
The ability for examination and discernment,
is the talent to distinguish the worthy from the unworthy.
Thus, in the court,
he is assistant to the Shīshì,
and for the state, governance is in censure and pruning.
Clear marking of right and wrong,
therefore he assists the Shīshì in judging good and bad.
The power of strength and boldness,
is the talent of the hero and outstanding man.
Therefore, in the court,
it is the responsibility of the Jiàngshuài,
and for the state, governance is strict and severe.
His physique is resolute and firm,
thus he commands the Six Armies and manifests military might.
As for people of partial talents,
each possesses a single excellence.
For example, candy is named for its sweetness,
while wine is essentially bitter.
Thus, one who excels in handling a single office,
like an archer skilled in shaping bow wood,
has energy to spare.
But is deficient in governing a whole state.
Overseeing both pottery and smelting,
the implements are not made well.
Why is this so?
The duty of a single office
is to harmonize one flavor with five flavors.
The salt master seasons the salt,
the vinegar master seasons the vinegar,
thus the five flavors are complete.
Like the carpenter working wood,
and the mason building walls,
the mansion is thus finished.
The governance of a state,
harmonizes five flavors with no particular flavor.
Water has no flavor,
thus it allows the five flavors to blend harmoniously.
Likewise, when the ruler’s disposition is bland and impartial,
all officials can exert their abilities.
Moreover, the state has its customs and culture,
the people have degrees of difficult or easy character,
the five regions differ,
and local customs vary.
The land may be hard or soft,
and the people difficult or easy.
Yet personal talents are different,
therefore governance can succeed or fail.
To rule simply in an easy situation brings success,
but governing with complexity brings failure.
Therefore, the governing method of royal transformation
is suitable for uniting the great;
using ease and simplicity, the order of the world is achieved.
Applying this to small matters,
is pedantic.
The net is wide-meshed and allows boat-sized wrongdoers to slip through.
The administration of litigation and defense
is suited to handling complex affairs;
when all matters are adjudicated,
disorder is then rectified.
To use this for easy governance,
then nothing is easy.
Being overly supervisory and urgent,
the people are inconvenienced.
The political strategy of plans and tactics
suits the governance of hardship,
where adaptability and resourcefulness
resolve disasters and crises.
Using this for peaceful times,
there is nothing extraordinary.
The complexity of arts and numbers is overwhelming,
the people feel unrest.
Oppositional and forceful government
is appropriate for restraining luxury;
excessive correction overreaches,
to check extravagance and debauchery.
Using this to govern corruption,
leads to harshness.
If harsh government addresses corruption,
the people are harmed.
Harmonizing government
suits newly established states;
where rituals are few,
and there is only loose conformity.
Using this for old states,
is hollow.
Such conformity is not grounded in true ritual.
The stern and exacting government
is fit for suppressing crime;
if the harshness is not deep,
wrongdoing and disorder do not end.
Used at the border,
it loses the masses.
The masses fear the law,
and are prone to escape or rebellion.
The government of awe and fierceness
is suitable for pacifying rebellion;
when the people are unruly and defiant,
only awe brings submission.
Applied in good times,
it becomes violent.
Harsh rule injures the people,
harming the good and honest.
The administration by skill and artifice
is suited to governing the wealthy;
it uses state strength on the people,
employing them.
Used for the poor,
it labors while the wealthy prosper and the poor suffer.
Frequent changes of goods and currency,
leave the people out of work.
Therefore, in assigning offices by ability,
one must be careful.
All these abilities
belong to persons of partial talent.
Thus, some can speak but not act,
some can act but not speak.
If intelligence prevails, one can speak;
if ability prevails, one can act.
But as for a person who embodies the state,
able both to speak and to act,
he is truly the elite among talents.
What distinguishes a ruler is his ability to differ from others in this regard.
He remains calm, indifferent, and does nothing,
so as to employ the abilities of the many.
Thus, a minister considers it his own ability to assume responsibility,
exhausting his strength to achieve merit,
and thereby gaining rank and title.
The ruler, however, sees the ability to use people as his own skill;
he employs the worthy and makes use of the capable,
and the state is thereby governed of itself.
A minister deems his skill to lie in eloquence,
each speaking of his own talents,
and thus receiving his office.
The ruler, for his part, sees his skill in listening;
he hears their words and observes their conduct,
and accordingly bestows office upon them.
A minister sees his skill in action,
and always acts on what he has said.
The ruler sees his skill in rewarding and punishing.
These must always correspond to merit or fault.
Each has different abilities;
the ruler does nothing, while the ministers have affairs to handle.
Therefore, he is able to govern and bring together the talents of many.
If the ruler himself undertakes to act
and replaces the master craftsman at carving,
then the various skilled artisans lose their cleverness,
and the work cannot be accomplished.
Advantages and Disadvantages, Chapter Six
Establishing laws and presenting methods,
to benefit the state.
But when their shortcomings appear,
the harm returns to oneself.
“Advantages and Disadvantages,” Chapter Six
The various pursuits among people
each have their own advantages and disadvantages.
As pursuits gradually lose their origin,
thus do advantages and disadvantages arise.
The pursuit of purity and integrity
is evident in one's bearing,
expressed through virtuous conduct.
When the mind is pure and the intentions upright,
then virtue and appearance manifest outwardly.
Before being employed, it is already apparent;
its way is harmonious and transformative.
When the radiance of virtue is illustrious,
there is efficacy without testing.
Its effect sets order among people,
hence all things are transformed by it.
Thus, when one has not yet distinguished oneself,
one is recommended by the multitude;
when principles are in accord, the multitude gladly promote such a person.
Once distinguished,
one is respected by both higher and lower ranks.
When virtue is harmonious and principles are in accord,
who could treat such a person with disrespect?
One’s achievements are sufficient to purge impurity and exalt purity,
serving as a model for officials and friends.
As a pursuit,
it is without flaw and constantly manifest;
not only is it without flaw,
but it persists and remains illustrious.
Therefore, it is valued by the world.
When virtue and trust are constant,
no one can belittle them.
The work of Fǎjiā
is based on institutions and systems,
awaiting success to become effective.
Law is used to prohibit crime;
when crime ceases, then it is effective.
Its doctrine is hardship in the beginning and order thereafter,
strict yet benefiting the masses.
At first, severity and authority are proclaimed;
thus comes toil and hardship;
in the end, governance is achieved through transformation by principle;
thus the people are governed.
Therefore, when it is not yet realized,
it is resented by the multitude;
criminal factions delight in disorder,
and many resent the law.
Once tested,
it is feared by superiors and inferiors alike.
Statutes and safeguards stand in solemn order,
causing both inner and outer circles to become alarmed.
Its achievements are sufficient to establish law and accomplish order;
the people do not do wrong,
and the way of order is fulfilled.
Its defect is that it becomes hated by groups of the unjust.
When the law is enforced, those favored and noble suffer,
and in the end they bring harm upon it.
Thus its practice has defects and is not constantly employed;
only an enlightened ruler can employ it forcefully;
