but enlightenment does not endure through generations,
so the law is not always used.
Therefore, the merit is great but does not last.
For this reason, Shāng Jūn was drawn and quartered,
and Wú Qǐ was dismembered.
The craft of the shùjiā arises from keen thought,
emerging from intelligence and reflection,
relying on attaining plans and making them manifest.
Its decisive points are determined before action begins;
when people lack trust,
only after achievement is accomplished and results are shown does it become apparent.
Its way is at first subtle, then becomes manifest,
refined and profound.
The stratagems are subtle and wondrous;
at the beginning, they reach utmost refinement,
and from start to finish they correspond,
thus the way becomes manifest.
Before its effects are realized,
it is not recognized by the multitude;
as strategy precedes achievement,
how could the masses recognize it?
In its use,
it is prized by an enlightened ruler.
When the ruler is benighted and ignorant,
how could he value it!
Its achievements suffice to plan and adapt to change;
by change, adaptability is sought,
thus its successes can be realized.
When withdrawn,
it hides in obscurity and subtlety.
Strategies arise from delicacy and secrecy,
thus they are not exposed.
As a profession,
it is rare and seldom employed;
the ruler's calculations are miraculous,
yet those who can utilize them are few indeed.
Therefore, sometimes it remains deep and subtle, not becoming manifest.
Few in the world can employ it;
how then can its way become manifest?
The work of Zhìyì originates from fundamental principles;
its way is smooth and without obstruction.
Complying with the times and circumstances,
how could there be any opposition?
Therefore, while it has not yet come to fruition,
it is accommodated among the common people;
affairs do not go against it,
and the virtuous draw near to it.
Once it has succeeded,
it receives praise and affection.
It harmonizes with the multitude,
admired both within and without.
Its achievements are enough to commend wise deliberation,
winning favor by conforming to the times,
and its plans and words are deemed trustworthy.
Its flaw, however,
lies in knowing how to advance and not knowing how to retreat,
failing to perceive resentment or harm,
thus ever longing for advancement.
Sometimes one strays from righteousness to preserve oneself.
By currying favor in thought,
one departs from what is right.
As an enterprise,
it is clever yet difficult to sustain.
Concealing feelings and displaying cleverness and intelligence,
it does not belong to the class of the truly upright and proper.
Thus sometimes profit comes first and harm follows.
Knowing to advance but forgetting to retreat
is the path to regret.
The work of Zāngfǒu
is rooted in right and wrong;
its way is upright and also corrective.
Pure and untainted,
it removes even the slightest impurity.
Thus, before it is recognized,
it is known among the people;
pure and unsullied,
it is clear even in obscurity.
Once it is recognized,
it becomes praised by the people.
Its principle is always evident,
and when made manifest, it is honored.
Its merit is sufficient to alter and discern right from wrong.
Its reasoning is clear and its way is upright,
so right and wrong are not confused.
Yet, its failure
is to become the object of slander and resentment.
The slanderers
do not enjoy hearing of their faults.
As for its operation,
it is severe and not generous;
exacting in judgment of things,
how can it be accommodating?
Thus, sometimes it gains an early advantage but later becomes isolated from others.
Its clarity is praised by the age,
but its severity is feared by the multitude.
The profession of skill and craft
is rooted in practical ability,
its methods are both precise and swift.
When skill and calculation are as wondrous as the spirits,
thus is swiftness and discernment achieved.
Before such skill is attained,
it is regarded as unusual by common people;
when skill surpasses the ordinary,
then, even if minor, it becomes conspicuous.
Once accomplishment is achieved,
one becomes entrusted by the authorities.
Thus affairs are successfully managed,
and such becomes the pursuit of governance.
Its merit is sufficient for managing complexity and rectifying wrongs.
To release from complexity or to rectify wrongs
also requires skill and craft.
Its shortcoming is that
the people are wearied and those below are exhausted.
When those above have many schemes, those below are afflicted.
As a profession,
it is detailed but not grand,
thus it is a minor element of governance.
When the Way is not balanced and broad,
how can abilities be truly great?
Understanding Connections, Chapter Seven
By putting oneself in the place of others and connecting with all things,
one comes to realize the unity of all beings.
Only those of exceptional ability
can thereby comprehend the talents of the multitude.
Section Seven: "Jiēshí"
It is truly difficult to know a person;
their appearance is sincere and their feelings are deep,
thus it is hard to understand them.
Yet scholars, regardless of their number,
all consider themselves adept at knowing others.
Therefore, they observe others through themselves,
and thus think them knowable.
If one esteems purity and integrity,
then everyone of purity and integrity is deemed someone they understand.
When observing how others assess people,
they believe those others are unperceptive.
Why is this so?
It is because what one values
lies in purity and integrity;
what others desire
lies in profit and desire.
If their standards differ from others’,
they immediately claim others do not understand people.
Thus, one can recognize the virtues akin to one’s own
and is naturally skilled in strategizing and planning,
making them a person proficient in strategy.
Yet they may miss the merits of those with different qualities.
Even those who strictly follow the law, though admirable,
are not acknowledged by the strategist’s assessments.
Why is this so?
The person of purity and integrity
uses uprightness as a measure,
and so when dealing with various talents,
can recognize the usual conduct of human nature.
Their standard is uprightness,
so they delight in people of constancy.
Yet they may suspect the artifice involved in administrative techniques.
They believe adhering to uprightness is enough to achieve good governance;
why, then, rely on techniques and arts of administration?
Those who are legalists
use measures and categories as their standard.
Thus, they are able to assess the capacities defined by rules;
their measure lies in legal divisions,
and therefore they are pleased with straightforward people.
Yet they do not value the art of adaptation.
They believe that measured rules are sufficient for the completion of affairs;
why, then, resort to cunning and stratagems?
Those who specialize in stratagem
take strategic planning as their criterion;
hence, they recognize extraordinary tactics,
value lies in strategic insight,
and so they esteem tacticians.
Yet they do not appreciate the excellence of those who abide by the law.
They say that plans and schemes suffice to transform the people;
why rely on law and institutions?
Those skilled in tools and techniques
use skill in defense and argument as their standard;
they consequently discern the rules of tactics,
and their value lies in argument and defense;
so they delight in those skilled at calculation.
Yet they do not understand the sources of institutions and regulations.
They claim tactical calculation surely enables achievement;
what is the use of institutions, then?
Those of discerning mind
use original intent as their measure;
thus, they can recognize those who possess concealed wisdom,
their measure is in original intent,
so they are pleased by people of hidden discernment.
Yet they do not value the constancy of law and instruction.
They claim original intent suffices for correctness;
why bother with legal principles, then?
Those skilled in cleverness and craft
measure all by the attainment of merit;
thus they recognize effective achievements,
their measure is in gaining merit,
and so they delight in the capable.
Yet they do not comprehend the transformation wrought by Dào Dé.
They assert that skill suffices to get things done;
what need is there for Dào Dé?
Those skilled in judgment
use observation and scrutiny as their rule;
therefore, they perceive the evidence for blame and correction,
and their standard is vigilance,
thus they are pleased with those apt at reproach and admonition.
Yet they do not allow for the diversity of the unconventional and unrestrained.
They say rebuke and admonition suffice for instruction;
why value tolerance and breadth, then?
Those skilled in discourse
take analysis and scrutiny as their measure;
thus, they perceive the wisdom in quick response,
and their standard lies in analysis,
so they delight in the quick-witted and responsive.
Yet they do not realize the beauty of concealed excellence.
They believe skill in argument suffices for handling affairs;
why pursue hidden excellence, then?
Therefore, they criticize and refute one another,
and none are willing to affirm each other.
Everyone considers themselves to be right,
and who is willing to acknowledge another’s correctness?
If they choose those of the same kind,
then they respond to each other and find harmony;
if their natures are even barely similar,
then even the Hú and Yuè,
by responding, can understand each other's feelings.
If they choose those of different kinds,
even after a long time, they do not understand each other.
If their natures are even slightly different,
then even if they are side by side,
after years, they become ever more estranged.
All cases of this type,
are said to be people of one stream.
Therefore, those of the same kind are close,
those of different kinds are distant.
If of the second degree and above,
each includes what it can encompass,
and thus attains diversity.
The Fǎjiā employ both law and technique,
and thus can use technique to assist law.
Thus, people of one stream,
can recognize the virtues of one stream;
those who govern by law,
always act without exceeding the law.
People of two streams,
can recognize the merits of two streams.
Those who embody both law and technique,
apply both law and technique together.
If someone possesses all streams,
then they can also be proficient in all kinds of talent.
If they embody all eight streams,
then the eight kinds of talent are all properly placed,
and nothing is left unregulated.
Therefore, people of comprehensive talent are in harmony with the structure of the state.
Speaking of those of the eight talents,
they begin to advance and offer their counsel.
The office of Zhǒngzǎi,
examines what they are able to do.
If one wishes to observe but a single corner of it,
then an entire morning is enough to understand it.
If one seeks to investigate it in detail,
then three days are required before it is sufficient.
What does it mean to require three days?
Within the body of the state, a person possesses three faculties,
thus, in discourse, less than three days is not enough to exhaust them.
The first is to discuss Dàodé,
the second is to discuss Fǎzhì,
the third is to discuss Cèshù,
only then can one fully reveal their strengths and raise them without doubt.
Those in higher positions must also be versed in the eight faculties,
only then can they fully employ those promoted without uncertainty.
If so, then how can one discern whether someone is broad or narrow in talent, and speak to them accordingly?
How can one recognize narrow talent by observing one’s words at the moment?
How can one recognize broad talent as well?
As for a person’s character,
if one constantly takes up and gathers the strengths of others and gives them titles accordingly,
this is being broad.
If one always classifies things according to affairs and lists all that people can do by name,
words become too numerous to utter.
For example, if one praises Chén for his beauty,
it is in hopes that others will praise him.
If one has something good, he will talk of it himself according to affairs,
and also hopes that others will often speak of his goodness.
If one does not wish to know the strengths of others, this is being narrow.
If others have good qualities,
one’s ears are not pleased to hear it;
when others praise them,
one’s mouth will not echo it.
If one does not wish to know others,
then there is nothing spoken that is not doubted.
If one hears about law, one suspects it of being harsh and trimming;
when one hears of methods, one suspects them of being cunning and deceitful.
Therefore, if one explains the profound with the shallow,
the more profound, the more it differs from the listener’s understanding.
What is shallow is close to one’s own ideas,
thus when the profound principle is heard, the mind becomes even more dazzled.
Thus when Shāng Jūn expounded the Way of the Emperor and was not accepted,
he instead presented the theory of strong armies.
When things are different, they contradict each other;
when contradicted, they mutually oppose.
When the profound is heard, the mind becomes dazzled;
how then can one affirm one another?
Therefore, Lǐ Duì blocked his ears and would not listen to Sū Qín’s arguments.
Thus, when someone often presents straightforward opinions,
it is taken as being admirable;
when one has many approaches,
it is suspected as seeming to be wonderful.
If one quietly listens without speaking,
this is taken for emptiness;
if one waits for the right moment then speaks,
it is suspected as being insubstantial.
If one speaks in lofty terms with a raised voice,
it is considered disrespectful;
if one’s words defend and reason at a high level,
it is suspected as being overbearing.
If one is not wholly yielding and modest,
it is considered shallow and uncouth;
if one’s words are humble and lacking vigor,
it is suspected as being superficial.
If one’s words mention a single good point,
it is deemed as being not broad;
if one dares not to present much,
it is suspected as being narrow and petty.
If someone expounds on many marvels,
it is taken as being full of intrigue;

If one speaks in anticipation of another’s thoughts,
it is considered as sharing one’s excellence;
if one’s words match another’s ideas,

If by chance one fails and is questioned,

if one wishes to make up for the failure,
one fails to be understood yet again.
If one debates by presenting opposing views,
it is regarded as competing with others;
if one purposely argues the opposite to clarify the matter,
it is still suspected as contesting.
If one’s discourse is broad but mixed and varied,
it is said to lack essentials.
If one pours out all that is in one’s heart,
it is said to lack essentials.
If one’s arguments are of the same kind,
then only is there pleasure.
When brothers quarrel bitterly,
they bring up the story of Guǎn and Cài,
and then rejoice and are pleased together.
At this moment, there is affection between them,
and they declare each other’s praises;
provided their words are alike,
it is not only affection,
but goes so far as to praise and recommend each other.
This is the common fault of narrow talent.
Their intention ever cherishes and protects,
wishing others to resemble themselves,
but even they themselves cannot wholly achieve it,
so how can they attain it even for a moment?
Heroes, Chapter Eight
Unless they are ordinary,
each is famed in his own way.
Yīng is renowned in civil affairs,
Xióng is distinguished in military matters.
“Heroes,” Chapter Eight
Among plants, what is most refined and outstanding is called yīng; among beasts, the one that stands out among its kind is called xióng.
If even things have this,
how much more so with people!
Thus, when people possess exceptional qualities in civility or martial prowess,
their names are derived from this.
Civil qualities take yīng as their name,
and martial qualities take xióng as their designation.
Therefore, one whose intelligence and outstanding talents stand out is called yīng,
and one whose courage and strength surpass others is called xióng.
These are the general distinguishing names.
If we compare their proportions,
they each require the other.
Yīng acquires a share of xióng,
and then becomes fully developed;
xióng acquires a share of yīng,
and then becomes truly strong.
Each possesses two parts,
taking one part from the other,
so that only then are they complete.
Courage is a part belonging to xióng,
intelligence is a part belonging to yīng.
Yīng possesses intelligence,
but only with courage can it be accomplished;
xióng possesses courage and strength,
but only with wisdom can it stand firm.
How can this be explained?
The intelligent and perceptive—
these are the qualities of yīng;
but without the courage of xióng,
one's plans cannot be carried out.
Wisdom without courage
cannot speak rightly.
Strength of courage—
this is the quality of xióng;
but without the intelligence of yīng,
undertakings cannot be established.
Bravery without strategy
cannot establish affairs.
Therefore, the yīng, with their intelligence, begin with strategy;
with their perception, they discern opportunity;
wisdom initiates planning of affairs,
perception catches the critical moment.
They wait for the courage of xióng to carry things out;
without decisiveness, action cannot proceed.
The xióng, with their strength, subdue the masses;
with their courage, they overcome difficulties;
without strength, people cannot be subdued;
without courage, difficulties cannot be overcome.
They wait for the intelligence of yīng to bring matters to completion.
Wisdom arranges what is fitting;
only then can skill bring about success.
Only then can each draw upon their strengths.
It is like gold, which depends on water to be refined into useful implements;
things require water before sustenance is accomplished.
If cleverness can initiate planning,
but perception fails to discern opportunity,
one can only discuss in theory,
but cannot deal with affairs in practice.
Wisdom may suffice for theoretical discourse,
but if perception cannot discern opportunity,
how can one manage matters at all?
If cleverness can start planning,
and perception can seize the moment,
but bravery cannot carry it out,
one may follow the usual course,
but not adapt to change.
Perception may suffice for routine,
but if bravery fails to act,
how can one respond to transformation?
If strength surpasses others,
but courage does not follow through,
one may be a man of strength,
but not yet a vanguard;
even if surpassing the group,
if daring and courage lack decisiveness,
how can one be a true leader?
If strength surpasses others,
and courage is sufficient to act,
but wisdom cannot resolve matters,
one can be the vanguard,
but not fit to be a general.
One may have the strength to lead the charge,
but if unprepared for the situation,
how can one command as a general?
Only if one can begin with intelligent strategy,
perceive opportunities,
and exercise decisive courage,
can one then be called yīng—
as Zhāng Liáng was.
If one’s strength surpasses others,
has the courage to act,
and possesses adequate wisdom to resolve affairs,
only then can one be called xióng—
such was Hán Xìn.
The qualities of their character differ;
they are judged by the preponderance of traits,
hence the names yīng and xióng are distinguished.
Zhāng Liáng excelled in intelligence and strategy;
Hán Xìn surpassed others in courage and daring.
Yet both possessed talents that tended toward partial excellence,
fitting for those who serve as officials.
Thus, yīng can serve as prime minister,
securing near victories.
The xióng can serve as general,
spreading might afar.
If one person
possesses both yīng and xióng,
he can endure for generations—
Gāozǔ and Xiàng Yǔ were such men.
Yet the portion of yīng surpasses that of xióng,
but yīng cannot be lacking.
With yīng, wisdom is achieved;
the wise can harness xióng;
how then can yīng be lacking?
When the portion of yīng is diminished,
then the wise depart from it.
Thus, Xiàng Yǔ possessed peerless strength,
was keen in adapting to change,
and his courage knew no equal;
he crossed the Jiāng River and burned his provisions.
Yet he could not heed nor gather the remarkable;
failing to employ even one Fàn Zēng,
thus the likes of Chén Píng all deserted to Gāo Zǔ.
When the portion of yīng is abundant,
therefore all the mighty submit to him,
and the talents of yīng gather to him;
both are put to use.
Once the mighty are subdued,
the yīng also come to him.
Hence, he could swallow Qín and vanquish Chǔ,
establishing his domain over All Under Heaven.
Thus, the abundance or scarcity of yīng and xióng
determines one's own power to overcome.
If victory lies within oneself,
then one can overcome all things.
If there is only yīng and no xióng,
then talents of might will not submit;
without an inner sovereign,
how can one attract that which is external?
If there is only xióng and no yīng,
the wise will not come.
Without a name to receive them,
how would the wise be drawn near?
Thus, the mighty can obtain the mighty,
but cannot obtain yīng;
rhinos and tigers form their own groups.
Yīng can gain the yīng,
but cannot gain the mighty;
luán birds and fèng birds flock together.
Therefore, when a single person
embodies both yīng and xióng,
only then can he command both yīng and xióng.
If he can command both yīng and xióng,
thus can he accomplish great undertakings.
With martial force he subdues them,
with civil virtue he pacifies them,
then his achievements will be renowned in his lifetime,
and fortune will flow to later generations.
Eight Observations, Ninth Section
Talents are of different types;
each ambition has a different destination.
Observing their success or failure,
there are eight categories to which they may be assigned.
“Eight Observations,” Chapter Nine
The Eight Observations are as follows:
First is to observe how one takes and gives relief,
to discern confusion and mixture;
sometimes one desires to offer compassion and aid, yet withholds it and thus deprives their own benevolence,
sometimes one gives broad and generous relief, yet asks for vinegar, taking it as a favor.
Second is to observe their response to changes,
in order to assess their usual measure;
by observing their anger or shame,
one can precisely judge their usual measure.
Third is to observe their genuine nature,
so as to know their reputation;
when evidence and nature respond to each other,
by looking at appearance, one may know the name.
Fourth is to observe their motives,
to distinguish dependence from resemblance.
Depending on exposure resembles honesty,
but it is difficult to discern swiftly;
examine in what they find ease,
then clarity naturally arises.
Fifth is to observe their love and respect,
to know their openness or obstruction;
with pure love, things draw close and feelings are communicated,
with pure respect, reasoning becomes estranged and feelings are blocked.
Sixth is to observe their emotional impulse,
to distinguish between forgiveness and confusion;
when obtaining what they desire, there is forgiveness,
when opposing their desire, there is confusion.
Seventh is to observe their shortcomings,
to know their strengths;
though being blunt and critical may be a shortcoming,
it is a strength in honesty.
Eighth is to observe their intelligence and clarity,
to know their attainments.
Though one possesses many talents,
if the talents lack intelligence and clarity,
matters become obstructed on all sides,
how then can one achieve anything?
What is meant by observing what is taken and what is rescued,
in order to clarify mixtures of motives?
For substance may reach its fullest or fall into deviation.
When the firm disposition is without desire,
this constitutes utmost attainment;
when greedy feelings sometimes prevail,
this constitutes deviation.
If utmost attainment is overcome by deviation,
then evil feelings take away the right,
appearing as though so, but not actually so.
When desire overcomes firmness,
this may seem like firmness, but is not firm.
Thus, rén arises from cí,
yet there are those who possess cí but not rén;
rén must necessarily include xù,
yet there are those who possess rén but not xù;
severity must have firmness,
yet there are those severe but not firm.
If upon seeing something pitiable one weeps,
this is the compassionate heart arising within.
But as they are about to share and give, they become stingy,
thus they are compassionate but not rén;
those who practice rén necessarily assist and relieve.
Upon witnessing danger and urgency, they feel compassion,
the feelings of rén stir within.
But about to rush to rescue, they fear calamity,
thus are rén but not xù;
those who relieve must rush to danger.
When occupying a position of righteous emptiness, they show severity in countenance,
the spirit of severity manifest in appearance.
But considering profit and desire, they are weak within,
thus are severe but not firm.
Those who are firm must be without desire.
Thus, if one is compassionate but not rén,
this is because stinginess has deprived it;
love of wealth damages compassion.
If one is rén but not xù,
this is because fear has deprived it;
timidity diminishes rén.
If one is severe but not firm,
this is because desire has deprived it.
Profit and desire harm firmness.
Thus it is said:
If compassion cannot overcome stinginess,
there is no certainty it can be rén;
if one loves but does not give,
how can rén be achieved?
If rén cannot overcome fear,
there is no certainty it can be xù;
if timidity and cowardice prevent decisiveness,
how can relief be practiced?
If severity cannot overcome desire,
there is no certainty it can be firm.
If feelings persist for profit and desire,
how can firmness be established?
Thus, when the substance of non-rén prevails,
then skills and strength become instruments of harm;
when the substance of rén is already weak but has skills and strength,
this is a tool that harms oneself.
When the nature of greed and disobedience prevails,
then strength and ferocity become a ladder to disaster.
When the substance of honesty is already defeated but the nature remains strong and fierce,
this is a ladder to one’s own ruin.
There are also cases where good feelings rescue evil,
so it does not reach harm,
but evil things ought to be cut off and removed;
those of pure goodness pity and rescue them,
such are thick and generous people,
not a great harm.
When love, favor, and sharing are deep,
even with pride and familiarity, they do not part.
In lifelong friendship,
if the bonds are deep and the ties strong,
even if Yuán Rǎng and Yí Sī wait but do not abandon each other,
there is no great fault.
Helping the good stands out clearly,
even if one hates evil,
there is no harm in this;
such as killing the unrighteous to achieve the righteous,
even if the hatred of evil is extreme,
it is not a great wrong.
If rescue and relief are excessive,
even if one takes from others,
it is not out of greed.
If one takes other people’s things in order to rescue and relieve,
even though criticized as begging for vinegar,
this is not great greed.
Therefore, observing what is taken and what is rescued,
one can know the feelings of mixture.
At times, fear and stinginess take away compassion and rén,
at times, rescue and relief exceed proper measure,
while the even-tempered ruler follows along and shows forgiveness.
What does it mean to observe one's feelings and changes,
so as to carefully discern their constant standard?
When a person possesses a refined appearance and deep feelings,
and seeks to obtain something,
one must observe their words and intentions,
and examine their responses and corroborations.
Consider the purpose behind their utterances,
and observe whether their responses are appropriate or not.
To observe the purpose of their words
is like listening to the quality of music;
once music is sung, its beauty or ugliness is distinguished.
To examine their responses and aid
is like assessing whether one's intelligence is sufficient.
With voices in harmony, ability or inability is clear.
Therefore, by observing words and examining responses,
it is enough to distinguish and recognize each other.
This one sets the tone and that one joins in,
and right and wrong are thus raised in contrast.
If in discourse one plainly expresses the upright,
this is clarity;
if in words one conspicuously sets the proper,
this is called being manifestly clear.
If one is unskilled in responding,
it is abstruse;
if silent while discerning it,
this is called the abstruse.
When the profound and the clear are interwoven,
this is comprehension;
when one can clearly distinguish right from wrong,
one may be said to understand principle.
If changes occur without any standard,
this is confusion;
when principle is not relied upon singly,
words and intentions are confused and mixed.
If one recognizes the not yet manifest in advance,
one is shèng;
when one reflects upon abstruse matters,
one is ruì;
perceiving things beyond others,
one is míng;
regarding clarity as obscurity,
one is zhì;
even though the mind is discerning,
one always feels it insufficient.
To recognize even the subtle and fleeting,
is miào;
though the principle be exceedingly fine,
yet one can perceive it.
When beauty and subtlety are not forgotten,
this is shū;
when the mind is manifestly attentive,
this is called shūlǎng.
The deeper one probes,
the more solid it becomes;
when the mind possesses true wisdom,
the more one investigates, the more refined;
like a spring that wells up from within,
the deeper one measures, the deeper it becomes.
When one displays a false facade with dazzling brilliance,
this is emptiness;
when one parrots hearsay and roadside talk,
over time there is no substance,
like pond water without a source,
which leaks and is depleted in vain.
To see only one's own excellence,
is deficiency;
when one's wisdom does not suffice,
one fears others do not know and thus boasts of oneself.
Not boasting of one’s ability
is superfluity.
He does not fear being unknown.
Therefore it is said:
Whenever affairs lack standard,
there must be a reason for it.
When appearance and complexion lose their reality,
there must be a cause of sorrow or joy.
The look of care and affliction
is weary and listless;
when worries and troubles are in the heart,
the appearance becomes gaunt.
The look of illness
is disturbed and without order.
When yellow and dark colors are mingled,
the features are filled with dust and dirt.
The look of joy is content and cheerful,
the look of anger is harsh and raised.
The color of jealousy and delusion
is reckless and inconstant,
coarse white and coarse red,
anger flushing the face.
As for their movements,
these too are expressed in words and demeanor.
When the look is already apparent,
the speech follows accordingly.
Thus, when one's words are extremely cheerful,
but the essential color does not follow,
there is discord within;
when the heart bears hatred but speech is forced to harmonize,
the appearance and countenance will never be in accord.
When words are contradictory
but the essential expression is trustworthy,
the speech is simply unskillful.
Words do not fully express;
thus, although words are at variance, expression and appearance may be relied upon.
When words have yet to be uttered but an angry look is first seen,
the emotion is overflowing with indignation;
when anger fills the chest,
even before speech the appearance is already revealed.
When words are uttered and anger is sent forth with them,
one is forcibly acting against what should not be;
desiring to force what ought not to be done,
thus the anger assists the speech.
In all such cases,
the evidence is apparent on the outside,
and cannot be completely concealed.
When the mind is happy but the face is angry,
when the heart resents but the appearance is harmonious,
even if one wishes to disguise it,
the essential color will not comply.
The heart moves, and the appearance is affected.
Astonishment and shock are clear,
and though change occurs, it can be perceived.
Though feelings are internal,
astonishment manifests outwardly.
A thousand forms and ten thousand expressions
can be roughly discerned.
Therefore, by observing one's feelings and changes,
the constant temperament can be known.
By observing a person's words and expression, one can know their heart;
when things have their constant measure,
only then is discernment complete.
What does it mean to observe one’s highest substance
in order to know its name?
In general, the nature of partial talents,
when the two utmosts or more are present,
the utmost substance mutually manifests,
and thus eminent names arise.
The two utmosts
refer to substance and energy.
When the substance is upright and the energy is pure,
then good names are produced.
Thus, when the bones are upright and the energy is pure,
honored reputations emerge;
when the bones and energy echo one another,
then names are thereby beautiful.
When the energy is pure and the strength is vigorous,
then illustrious names arise;
once the energy is pure,
if the strength is vigorous, then the fame is illustrious.
When strength, intelligence, refinement, and reason all cohere,
then capable reputations arise;
when intelligence is already strong,
and reason is refined, then one is called capable.
When intelligence is upright, resolute, and sincere,
then a reputation for responsibility is born.
When uprightness is also beautiful,
thus one becomes trusted with responsibilities.
When all gather at the purest essence,
then exemplary virtue is achieved;
when the substance is refined, just, and harmonious,
then good virtue is accomplished.
If one adds learning,
then culture and reason shine forth.
Gui jade has substance;
when polished, it gains patterns.
Therefore, by observing the measure of one’s utmost attainment,
the origin of different reputations may be known.
Seek the inherent substance and energy,
examine their clarity or turbidity;
though there are differences in quantity,
and variety of forms in names,
one can surely know the distinctions.
What does it mean to observe the origin of a thing
in order to distinguish what only appears similar?
If one is purely critical by nature,
and cannot be just and fair,
and both character and temperament are wholly critical,
what uprightness can be found in that?
Derivative harshness appears as uprightness,
using critique to seem virtuous;
and if uprightness becomes harsh,
critique even reaches the good.
Pure wildness resembles being unrestrained,
but cannot communicate the Way;
if both character and temperament are wholly wild,
how could the Way be communicated?
Derivative wildness seems communicative,
but conducts itself arrogantly and exceeds proper bounds.
Apparent communication that is really wildness
indulges arrogance without restraint.
Thus it is said:
the upright can also be harsh,
the harsh are certainly harsh,
their harshness is the same,
yet their basis for being harsh is different;
the harshness of the upright
rebukes evil and shuns wrongdoing;
the pure harshness is simply harsh,
and criticizes even the good.
The communicative are sometimes wild,
and the wild are certainly wild,
their wildness is the same,
but their basis for being wild is different.
The wildness of the communicative
is simple and reaches the Way.
Pure wildness is arrogant, eccentric, and self-indulgent.
Then how can we distinguish them?
To be upright and yet gentle—
that is virtue;
gentleness and harmony bring uprightness,
and that is what makes virtue.
To be upright and like to criticize—
that is partiality;
if uprightness inclines to harshness,
that is why it is partial.
To be critical but not upright—
that is derivative;
pure harshness appears upright,
and thus becomes derivative.
To be guided by the Way and able to restrain oneself—
that is communication;
using the Way to restrain oneself—
that is what makes communication.
Communicative yet sometimes excessive—
that is partial;
if the nature to communicate is sometimes excessive,
so is partiality.
To be wild but unrestrained—
that is derivative;
pure wildness appears communicative,
thus it is derivative.
Partiality and derivativeness
have like aims but different substance,
what is called "seeming so but not so."
The same substance produces communication and uprightness,
but sometimes partial or derivative.
Thus one who readily promises seems resolute but lacks trustworthiness,
overestimates himself,
makes casual promises to the dead,
yet when facing danger becomes fearful,
and cannot sacrifice himself.
One quick to take things up seems capable but lacks results,
does not consider his talents and abilities,
boasts he can manage,
seeks tasks rashly,
and produces no effective result.
Eager advancement seems diligent but is too fleeting,
such impatient people
cannot hold posts for long.
One who demeans others seems discerning but is troublesome,
and those who scold and blame
cause much chaos.
A harsh favor seems kind but never succeeds,
for the moment there is help,
but it achieves nothing in the end.
One who agrees to your face seems loyal but is unfaithful behind your back,
yielding in the moment,
but asserting themselves when behind.
These are types of seeming so but not so.
Purple disturbs cinnabar red,
and sages dislike it.
There are also things that seem not but truly are:
things that appear like not,
but whose achievements are real.
Great authority may seem wicked but brings merit,
as Yī expelled Tài Jiǎ
to accomplish his task.
Great wisdom may seem foolish but is clear within,
never erring all day,
making subtle distinctions within.
Universal love may seem superficial but is truly profound,
broadly loving and without selfishness,
seeming empty but actually true.
Upright words may seem harsh yet are sincerely loyal.
Take Dì Jié and Zhòu for instance,
they were completely loyal and loving.
Discernment may appear to be false understanding,
with a contrary approach to controlling feelings,
seeking to discern what is similar,
and dividing right from wrong,
guiding people's feelings,
repeatedly clarifying them.
Somewhat like adjudicating a lawsuit,
it is truly difficult to distinguish.
Thus the sage conducts wide inquiries and asks broadly,
sharing decisions with all.
Without the greatest discernment under heaven,
who can grasp the reality?
If the reality could be easily grasped,
why worry about Huān Dōu?
Why bother with Yǒu Miáo?
Thus, waking at dawn,
he reveals the obscure and lowly,
consults Sān Huái,
and inquires of Jiǔ Jí.
Listening to words and trusting appearance,
one may lose the truth;
awkward speech and an unpleasant appearance,
even Zhòngní misjudged Zǐyǔ.
Twisted feelings and reversed judgments,
sometimes obscure worthy men.
Suspecting things beyond human emotion,
Gōngsūn misjudged Bǔ Shì.
The discernment of worth or not
truly lies in what they are based on.
Though difficult to understand,
one should always search for their basis and discern accordingly.
Therefore, by observing the basis,
the substance underneath seeming likeness may be known.
Though one may not fully grasp the reality,
yet by examining the basis of seeming likeness,
their bodies and dispositions—
one may come close to understanding them.
What is meant by observing one's love and respect
in order to discern openness or obstruction?
Indeed, to the utmost of the human way,
nothing surpasses love and respect.
Love arises from the relationship between father and son,
while respect is established between ruler and minister.
Therefore, the Xiàojīng esteems love as the highest virtue,
originating from the intimacy of father and son;
thus it is the supreme virtue.
It takes respect as the essential way;
ending with the righteousness between ruler and minister;
therefore, it is the essence of the Way.
The Yì regards responsiveness as virtue,
vital energy circulates and gives birth to living things,
from which people benefit and nourish themselves.
It takes humility as the Way;
the distinction between high and low is clearly set,
which is the order of the Way.
Lǎozǐ esteems non-action as virtue,
and its transformation is delivered without constraint,
such is the pattern of virtue.
He takes emptiness as the Way.
Serene, tranquil, and without action:
this is the principle of the Way.
Rites take respect as their foundation;
rites are enacted by yīn,
solemn and pure.
Music takes love as its core;
music arises from yáng,
joyous and affectionate.
Thus, the substance of human feelings,
when sincere in love and respect,
already exists in infancy,
where love and respect are born.
Thus, they share one body with the Way and Virtue;
their movement captures the human heart,
and thus the Way is unimpeded in every respect.
Embody the Way and cultivate virtue;
thus things align with reason and flow.
Yet love cannot be less than respect.
If it is less than respect,
then only those of integrity are drawn to it;
upright people cherish respect,
so they are drawn to it.
But the majority do not associate with it;
people delight in love,
if love is lacking,
they do not participate.
If love exceeds respect,
then even those of integrity are not pleased,
but those who are easily attached by affection would give their lives for it.
Upright people are few,
but common people are many.
When many people, delighted by love, dedicate themselves entirely,
then achievement and success follow.
Therefore, the Way of love
must not be diminished.
Why is this?
The Way of respect
is austere and distances people,
so its influence is hard to last long;
actions must always be solemn,
and this does not endure for long.
Travelers at an inn
depart before warmth and harmony can be established.
As for the Way of love,
affections are intimate, intentions sincere and deep,
and it profoundly moves things.
Warm and genuine, sincere and close,
it stirs others deeply, deeply indeed.
Thus, even mulberry gatherers
would turn their spears to repay kindness.
Therefore, by observing the sincerity of one's love and respect,
the reason for openness or obstruction can be discerned.
If one is devoted to compassion and love,
then warmth and harmony will flow between the upper and lower ranks;
if one puts all effort in practicing courtesy and respect,
then formality prevails, and communication between inside and outside is blocked.
Therefore, love and respect must mutually assist each other,
and neither can be absent even for a moment.
But for those who practice both principles,
one should always strive to make love greater and respect lesser;
only then may a solemn and majestic atmosphere be seldom encountered.
What is meant by observing the machinery of one’s emotions,
in order to discern the sources of forgiveness and confusion?
The emotions of people possess six mechanisms:
When one is gratified in what one desires, there is joy.
When a person of strength praises Wū Huò,
none can but be delighted at heart.
When one is not gratified in what one is able, there is resentment;
when a person eloquent and quick-witted is commended as Sān Jiān,
their hearts cannot but be indignant.
When one boasts of oneself and puts others through it, there is aversion;
one asserts one’s own abilities,
and uses them to supplant others,
which is what all detest.
If one yields and humbles oneself beneath another, there is delight;
lowering and humbling oneself before others,
all will be pleased and joyful.
When one exposes another's shortcomings, there is anger;
people all rejoice in their strengths,
and hate that which is their weakness.
Thus, when one points out another’s weak points,
there is resentment, hostility, and unrestrained anger.
When aversion meets resentment, there is jealousy.
Boasting of one's own abilities —
this is what others dislike;
calling out others' weaknesses —
this is what angers others.
Now if one boasts of one's abilities
and exposes what angers others,
then jealousy and harm are born.
These are the six mechanisms of human emotion.
Human nature is such that none do not wish to fulfill their ambitions;
the desires of the will,
if fulfilled, bring satisfaction.
Thus, the resolute person finds joy in feats of daring,
and when troubles come, the mighty strive forth.
The virtuous man delights in instructing good governance,
and when government is rectified, the virtuous are employed.
The capable delight in restoring order to chaos,
and in times of disorder seek the worthy and able.
The strategist delights in schemes and counsel,
and when plans abound seeks out their stratagems.
The debater delights in the keen exchange of words,
and when made a guest or assistant yearns to display eloquence.
The greedy delight in the accumulation of riches,
and when wealth is amassed,
the greedy are eager to pursue it.
The fortunate delight in holding power and prestige above all.
When power and prestige are preeminent,
the fortunate will secretly seize control.
If one supports another’s ambition,
none will fail to rejoice.
This is what is meant by gratifying what is desired,
and then there is joy;
the desires of the heart, once gratified entirely,
what grievance then remains?
If one is not gratified in what one is able,
then one’s ambition is not attained;
when one’s ambition is not attained,
there is sorrow.
One worries that one’s talents will not unfold.
Thus, when merit is not established,
the resolute will strive;
to strive,
is to be angry that one cannot fully realize one’s talents.
If virtue is not taught,
the upright grieve;
to grieve,
is to lament that one cannot practice one’s influence.
When government is chaotic and ungoverned,
the able sigh;
to sigh,
is to regret that one cannot use one’s talents.
When worthy rivals are not tamed,
strategists worry;
to worry,
is to fret that one cannot employ one’s ingenious plans.
If riches are not amassed,
the greedy fret;
to fret,
is to lament having nowhere to receive profit.
If power and prestige are not eminent,
the fortunate grieve.
To grieve,
is to bewail having no opportunity to wield power.
This is what is meant by not being gratified in one’s abilities,
and thus there is resentment.
If what one resents is not gratified, how can one rejoice?
Human nature is such that all wish to be at the fore,
thus people hate those who boast.
All wish to take the lead,
and so they dislike those who boast.
Boasting,
is about the desire to surpass others.
Thus, if one boasts of one’s excellence,
none will fail to dislike it.
They resent the intention to surpass them.
This is what is meant by boasting and putting others to the test,
and so there is aversion.
Therefore the enlightened never boast.
People all desire to prevail,
hence they are pleased by the humility of others.
In humility, one concedes to others,
and in yielding, there is an intention to give way.
Therefore, with people, noble or base,
if approached with humility,
there will be no lack of cheerful faces.
Ability aside,
all wish to surpass others.
Thus, humbling oneself to others
brings delight.
This is why the gentleman is always modest and yielding.
People all wish to conceal their shortcomings,
and have their strengths acknowledged.
When their strengths are praised, they are pleased;
when their faults are pointed out, they are angered.
Thus, when people criticize one’s weakness,
it feels as if one is being overborne.
The repression and vexation of emotion
is as if weight is laid upon one.
This is called exposing another’s weakness,
and thus, anger arises.
When oppression is sustained continuously,
the heart becomes resentful and hostile.
Human nature tends to look down on others.
Seeing another surpass oneself,
all wish to put them down.
If one offends that which others loathe,
even if one is hated,
it causes no great harm.
Though people dislike those who boast,
it does not deeply harm them.
But if one uses one’s strengths to attack another’s weakness,
this is what is called aversion encountering anger,
and so there is jealousy.
Using one’s strengths
to attack another’s weaknesses,
and thereby bringing harm upon oneself,
is precisely why the enlightened do not act thus.
Of all these six mechanisms,
their tendency is always to seek preeminence.
The self-importance of things—
it is so with everyone.
So the gentleman, in relating to others,
is willing to bear offenses without fuss.
Understanding that people love to outdo each other,
even if they are slightly affronted,
he will not get entangled or reject others.
Without disputing,
he always treats inferiors with respect,
and so avoids harm.
Practicing humility and respect,
who would harm him?
The petty person is not so,
for he does not perceive these mechanisms
and does not grasp the machinery of jealousy and harm.
Yet he wishes for others to be obedient,
and expects people to never go against him.
Feigning affection and respect, he sees any difference as betrayal;
Kǒng Guāng hesitated,
Dǒng Xián rejoiced.
If meetings happen by chance, he takes them lightly,
saying they are not heartfelt,
and resents being slighted.
If his mechanism is transgressed,
he grows deeply resentful.
The petty man is easily pleased yet hard to serve.
Therefore, by observing the machinery of emotion,
one may know the ambitions both noble and base.
The noble and enlightened have their aspirations in humility;
the base and ignoble set their aims on surpassing others.
Therefore, the unimposing ruler
governs with rectitude,
instructs the greedy on what makes them worry,
warns the fortunate on what brings them sorrow.
Then no one boasts of themselves,
those below do not put themselves above,
the worthy and unworthy find their proper place,
and the way of good government is set in order.
What does it mean to observe one’s shortcomings
in order to understand one’s strengths?
Those who possess partial talents
all have their own deficiencies.
Wisdom cannot be complete.
Thus, the fault of the upright lies in bluntness;
when bluntness becomes injurious to righteousness,
if the father steals a sheep,
the son testifies against him.
The fault of the resolute is severity;
when severity cuts against reason,
if remonstrating with the ruler fails,
he responds with the sword.
The fault of the harmonious is timidity;
when timidity falls short of the Way,
Gōngzhī Qí was timid among men,
and could not remonstrate with strength.
The fault of the unyielding is rigidity.
When rigid and foolish, one cannot manage affairs;
Wěi Shēng, holding fast to faith,
died beneath the bridge.
If a person is upright yet not blunt,
he cannot achieve uprightness;
if one delights in his uprightness,
one cannot fault his bluntness.
To employ a person’s uprightness
is to tolerate his bluntness.
Bluntness
is the mark of uprightness.
Without bluntness, one cannot be upright.
If a person is resolute but not severe,
he cannot complete his resoluteness;
if one delights in his resoluteness,
one cannot fault his severity.
To employ a person’s resoluteness
is to tolerate his severity.
Severity
is the mark of resoluteness.
Without severity, one cannot be resolute.
If a person is harmonious but not timid,
he cannot preserve his harmony;
if one delights in his harmony,
one cannot fault his timidity.
To employ a person’s harmony
is to tolerate his timidity.
Timidity
is the mark of harmony.
Without timidity, one cannot be harmonious.
If one is unyielding but not rigid,
he cannot uphold his unyielding nature;
if one delights in his unyielding nature,
one cannot fault his rigidity.
To employ a person’s unyielding nature
is to tolerate his rigidity.
Rigidity
is the mark of unyieldingness.
Without rigidity, one cannot be unyielding.
Yet, having shortcomings
does not necessarily mean having strengths;
a person wholly blunt
may yet not be upright.
One who has strengths
must reveal them by means of shortcomings.
One wholly harmonious
is sure to reveal timidity.
Therefore, by observing the mark of one’s shortcomings,
the strength of his talent can be known.
If you wish to employ his resoluteness,
you must draw it from his severity.
What does it mean to observe one's intelligence and understanding
in order to know their attainments?
Benevolence (rén)
is the foundation of virtue;
it is to carry virtue in action.
Righteousness (yì)
is the rule of virtue;
it prescribes what is fitting for virtue.
Ritual (lǐ)
is the adornment of virtue;
ritual,
is the pattern and principle of virtue.
Trustworthiness (xìn)
is the firmness of virtue;
firmness
is what virtue abides in.
Wisdom (zhì)
is the leader of virtue.
Without wisdom, virtue is not complete.
Wisdom arises from clarity;
only with clear understanding is one truly wise.
Clarity in a person
is like the day dependent on the sun,
or the night reliant on firelight.
The sun and fire illuminate day and night;
insightful understanding illuminates the principles of things.
The brighter the clarity,
the farther one can see.
The brighter the sun or fire,
the farther their light reaches;
the more penetrating the understanding,
the deeper the principles it comprehends.
The difficulty lies in clarity that reaches far;
even sages (shèngrén) may fall short in this.
Therefore, guarding one's profession and diligent study
may not necessarily match innate talent;
those born with understanding are the highest,
those made capable through study are next.
Skill and artifice, though refined and clever,
may not reach true principle;
those made skillful through practice
are often shallow in the highest principle.
To be quick at distinguishing right and wrong,
does not guarantee wisdom;
settling principle may achieve undertakings,
yet remain ignorant of profound wisdom.
Ability and intelligence may govern affairs,
but may not reach the Dao (dào).
Using intelligence to manage tasks
departs far from the Dao.
The Dao, with mysterious and far-reaching thought,
only then is it all-encompassing.
The Dao carries all things;
therefore, it is all-encompassing.
Thus, study cannot match talent,
talent cannot match principle,
principle cannot match wisdom,
wisdom cannot match the Dao.
The Dao and wisdom are mysterious and subtle,
therefore only after four transformations can they be reached.
The Dao
is cyclical, returning and adapting.
Principles are not fixed in one way,
thus there is transformation and adaptation.
Therefore, when considered separately,
each follows its own path;
then benevolence is supreme.
The benevolent are a resource to benefit others;
those with clarity merely perceive things.
But when combined and used together,
clarity takes the lead.
The benevolent rely on clarity,
and only then can their achievements be realized.
Therefore, when clarity leads benevolence,
there is none who is not embraced;
use authority to direct them,
benevolence to care for them.
When clarity leads righteousness,
there is none who is not overcome;
show them the proper distinctions and appropriateness.
When clarity leads principle,
there is nothing that is not understood.
If principle is clear and well practiced,
all matters are accomplished.
Therefore, without intelligence and clarity,
one cannot achieve success.
The dim and ignorant miss their time;
how can they ever succeed or accomplish anything?
Thus, to delight in fame but lack substance,
if one cannot fulfill, then one becomes empty;
emptiness drifts far from substance.
To delight in argument and reasoning,
if one does not reach the mark, then there is confusion;
confused words lack right principle.
To delight in laws and reflection,
if not deep, then one becomes harsh;
harshness exceeds principle.
To delight in technique and calculation,
if deficient, then one becomes deceitful.
Deceit is trickery and falsehood.
Therefore, when talent is balanced with a love of learning,
the enlightened become teachers;
when strength is matched in competition,
the wise become leaders.
When virtue is equal and all things are in order,
the accomplished are called sages (shèngrén).
The title "sage"
is the ultimate name for clarity and wisdom.
Thus, when they act, they become a model for the world;
when they speak, they become an exemplar for ten thousand generations;
in a high position, they are not arrogant;
in a low position, they are not disheartened.
Therefore, by observing one's intelligence and understanding,
the capacities they have attained can be known.
The Ten Kinds of Errors, Chapter Ten
The principles of human beings
are subtle and difficult to comprehend.
When examined by sentiment,
there are still seven errors.
“Seven Errors,” Chapter Ten
The Seven Fallacies:
First, there is the fallacy of biased discernment of praise,
where the evidence is unclear,
thus what is heard is partial.
Second, there is the confusion of affection and aversion in dealings with others,
sometimes, when feelings are alike, one forgets their faults,
sometimes, when intentions differ, one refutes their merits.
Third, there is the error of evaluating the mind in terms of smallness or greatness,
sometimes, little knowledge leads to no great accomplishment,
sometimes, meager understanding leads to no great insight.
Fourth, there is the doubt of early or late maturity in quality,
there are those who are wise early and achieve quickly,
and those whose wisdom comes late and achieve late.
Fifth, there is the suspicion of sameness in different types,
when abilities are equal and positions balanced, they compete with each other,
when abilities are equal but positions unequal, they respect each other.
Sixth, there is the ruse of enhancing or suppressing talent in discussions,
when relying on wealth and nobility, one dispenses favors and thus magnifies their reputation,
when living in poverty and humility, one begs for help and thus diminishes their reputation.
Seventh, there is the error of seeking out the extraordinary, with two particular faults.
The rare fault lies in concealment,
the blatant fault lies in empty extravagance,
thus discernment is hard to achieve.
As for the essentials of investigation and inquiry,
the point does not lie in how much is gathered.
Whether affairs are great or small,
what matters is attaining correctness.
Yet when evidence and substance are unclear,
one trusts the ear and dares not trust the eye.
The eye cannot discern,
thus the ear is believed.
Thus, when others judge something to be right,
the mind follows along and clarifies it;
when others judge it to be wrong,
the mind turns and transforms it.
Trusting others' blame and praise,
what was previously considered right
is transformed into being considered wrong.
Even when there is no suspicion,
the mind seems to harbor doubt.
For those who trust in others' blame and praise,
though in their hearts they have no suspicion,
yet in mind they remain doubtful.
Moreover, when people observe things,
there is also error within themselves.
Love and hate are mixed within,
their feelings have countless sources.
When one’s understanding cannot discern,
and is further compounded by love, dislike, right, and wrong,
how can these doubts be counted?
If the root is not made clear,
how can one be certain in trusting?
When the emotions of love and hate are removed,
then the truth is attained.
Therefore, one who knows people
uses the eye to correct the ear;
though listening to others' words,
always verifies them with the eye.
One who does not know people
relies on the ear and fails the eye.
Even when witnessing sincerity firsthand,
they still trust slander and discard it.
Thus, among the scholars of a district,
all either praise or all slander;
this cannot be taken as correctness.
Sometimes the majority are attached and form factions,
sometimes one stands alone and is not like the rest.
Among friends and associates,
when praise does not circulate three times,
it is not certain to be trusted as truth.
When forming bonds, and praise has not circulated three times,
one judges by appearance,
but the conduct does not match.
As for those with genuine and profound character,
among friends and companions,
they will always have someone speak of them favorably wherever they go.
Their words are loyal and trustworthy,
their actions earnest and respectful,
even in the lands of the Mán and Mò,
they will make their way.
The upper ranks extend support for them,
while the lower ranks recommend them.
If even the Mán and Mò recommend them,
how much more so in one’s own district!
If one cannot gain universal approval,
there will surely be reproach or slander.
Those whose actions are not earnest and respectful,
may flatter and gain favor with superiors but lose the lower ranks,
or attach themselves to factions below and lose the superiors.
Thus, if one inclines to the top and loses the bottom,
there will eventually be slander;
when those who criticize are many,
one cannot last.
If one inclines to the bottom and loses the top,
advancement will not be exceptional.
Though many among the common people recommend one,
the superiors do not trust such differences.
Therefore, if one’s sincerity can gain approval throughout thrice,
one will benefit the state,
and this is the upright friendship.
Because it is upright,
the reputation is thus beneficial.
Thus, even when all agree and say it is right,
there may still be dissenters;
some may deviate from principle and form factions,
thus all agree and declare it right.
Even when all agree and say it is wrong,
someone may be among them.
If one stands apart from the crowd,
all may agree and declare it wrong.
If there is one of remarkable and extraordinary talent,
such a person is not seen by the masses,
being outstanding and unique,
how could the masses recognize them?
Yet what the ear hears and gathers,
takes quantity as trustworthiness.
If one cannot carefully examine the person’s ability,
and only trusts the opinion of the many,
this leads to errors in judging fame.
When one trusts words to judge people and things,
there will surely be many mistakes and errors;
therefore, when the sage is to praise someone,
they must first put them to the test.
To love what is good and to hate what is evil—
this is the constant disposition of human nature.
Whether wise or foolish,
all share this same feeling.
If one does not clearly discern the substance,
one may be distant from what is good,
regarding good as not good.
Those who deny what is good,
when they see virtue, see it as distant.
Is this so of necessity?
It is because their understanding is not clear.
How can this be explained?
Those who deny goodness, although they reject it,
yet have that which they affirm.
Even if there are a hundred faults,
there must be one merit.
According to what they affirm,
conforming to their own strengths,
they recognize in others a single virtue
which is the same as their own strength.
Thus, without realizing it, their feelings are connected and their intentions close,
and they suddenly forget that person's faults.
Because of this similarity with themselves,
they forget the hundred faults,
and call a usurping son the height of filial piety,
or a leftover peach the height of loyalty.
Even a person of virtue, though virtuous,
may yet have some deficiency.
Even if there are a hundred virtues,
there may still be a single shortcoming.
By focusing on this deficiency,
and not discerning their own strengths,
they seize upon a single flaw in the virtuous person,
because it differs from their own strengths.
Because of their own strengths,
they slight their own weaknesses,
and thus, without knowing it, their resolve diverges and their temperament opposes,
suddenly forgetting the other’s virtue.
Because it differs from themselves,
they cast aside all a hundred virtues,
calling a crooked staff a dagger,
or a shield used for burial a tool of rebellion.
This is to be deluded by love and hate.
Those whose discernment is dim and obscure,
in dealing with others, are constantly led astray from that which is right by love or hate.
As for refinement, it should be profound and subtle;
character should be noble and weighty;
ambition should be broad and great;
the mind should be humble and small.
Subtlety in refinement
is that by which one enters into the realm of spirit and marvel;
coarseness causes the loss of the spirit.
Nobility and gravity
are that by which one exalts the mansion of virtue;
restlessness leads to the loss of one's self.
Great ambition
is that by which one conquers things and shoulders responsibilities;
if it is small, it cannot prevail.
A small mind
is that by which one is cautious against blame and regret;
if it is large, it becomes arrogant and overbearing.
Thus, in the Shī, when it sings of Wén Wáng,
“careful and vigilant,”
“not raising the voice nor coloring the face”—
this is the smallness of mind;
meaning he did not covet great fame nor display himself in appearance.
“The king is mightily angered,”
“facing all under Heaven”—
this is greatness of ambition.
Thus he could punish Zhòu,
settle all under Heaven,
and thus bring about great peace.
From this reasoning,
those whose mind is small and ambition great
are the kindred of sages and worthies;
the mind is small,
thus able to serve the Yīn;
ambition is great,
thus possessing two-thirds of the world.
Those whose mind is great and ambition great
are the outstanding among heroes;
with great ambition and great mind,
thus they are called heroic and eminent.
Those whose mind is great and ambition small
belong to the class of arrogant and dissipated;
small ambition with a mind broad and far-reaching,
thus they are the type of the arrogant and dissipated.
Those whose mind is small and ambition small
are constrained and timid people.
When the mind is near and ambition short,
how can one become broad and great?
The discernment of the multitude
sometimes disparages smallness of mind:
seeing Pèi Gōng burned and severed the Zhàn Road,
they said he could not unify all under Heaven.
Others esteem greatness of ambition:
seeing Xiàng Yǔ declare himself the mighty Chǔ,
they straightaway said he was fit to set right the feudal lords.
This is to err concerning smallness and greatness.
Because wisdom cannot discern their measure,
the mind is ever mistaken regarding smallness and greatness.
Human talent is not the same;
in achievement, there is early and late.
Some have early intelligence and mature quickly;
their nature is pure and their spirit is bright.
When they are born, they are outstanding and extraordinary.
Thus, Tóng Wū and Cāng Shū
displayed their brilliance even in childhood.
Some have late intelligence and mature late;
their nature is weighty and their spirit is slow.
It takes a long time before they become vessels;
thus, Gōngsūn Hándào
only became illustrious in old age.
There are those who have no intelligence in youth and achieve nothing in the end;
their nature is turbid and their spirit is dark.
They grow old without accomplishment;
thus, Yuán Rǎng in his old age,
even when questioned on the shins by the Sage, could not be transformed.
There are those who possess fine talent in youth and thus become remarkable vessels.
As children, they are perceptive and reasoned;
as they grow, they become ever clearer.
Thus, ordinary talent revealed the extraordinary in Yìng Bīn
and emulated virtue in Gōng Xiāng.
The principles of these four types
cannot go unexamined.
One should observe whether their achievement comes early or late
and employ them according to the times.
As for those with early intelligence,
their talent and wisdom are keen and penetrating;
even as children, all have discernible beginnings.
Zhòngní played at arranging sacrificial vessels;
Dèng Ài pointed at maps to discuss military campaigns.
Thus, if a child's language is rich in style,
if a child's words are abundant,
he will surely be elegant in writing when grown.
If debate is clever from the beginning,
if a child speaks quickly and fluently,
he will surely be capable of debate as an adult.
Benevolence issues from kindness and sympathy;
if a child is kind and sympathetic,
he will surely be compassionate when grown.
Generosity is shown by giving beyond measure;
if a child is overly generous,
he will surely love to give when grown.
Caution arises from fear;
if a child is often fearful,
he will surely be prudent as an adult.
Integrity comes from refusing to take what is not due.
If a child does not take things arbitrarily,
he will surely be honest and upright when grown.
Those with early intelligence are shallow and quick-witted,
quick to perceive and express small matters.
Those who mature late have profound insight but act slowly;
though their intelligence grows slowly,
they are able to grasp the subtle.
Those who are ever dull are always troubled by inadequacy;
when facing both difficult and easy matters,
their thoughts are always confused.
Those who are diligent in their affairs are thorough and even have surplus capacity.
No matter how great or small the matter,
they can always see it through.
But common people's judgments
do not take change into account;
they always generalize,
requiring consistency from beginning to end.
Thus, they are perplexed by differences between early and late maturity.
Some harbor doubts about those who mature late because of those who mature early,
and some suspect those who mature early because of those who mature late.
Thus, regarding people's natures,
there is often error and misjudgment.
As for human nature, none do not pursue fame and profit,
and avoid harm.
The path to fame and profit
lies in the attainment of what is right;
this attainment depends on oneself,
and thus fame and profit come.
The source of harm
lies in the pursuit of what is wrong and in loss.
Pursuit of what is wrong and loss also depends on oneself,
thus harm assails one.
Therefore, among people, whether worthy or foolish,
all wish that the attainment of what is right rests with themselves.
If even the worthy are thus,
how much more so the foolish?
The ability to clarify what is right in oneself
is surpassed by nothing more than the sense of shared nature.
If another’s nature is the same as mine,
then I am able to recognize myself.
Therefore, people with partial abilities,
those who make associates and join in pursuits,
all cherish and esteem those of shared nature and praise them,
for those of shared nature can clarify oneself,
thus they become close and praiseworthy.
Those whom they hate are contrary and they denounce them;
those whose nature is contrary to theirs,
thus they dislike and estrange them.
Those whose order is different and mixed are not esteemed.
If one is neither shared with oneself
nor contrary to oneself,
then even if not hated,
still they are not esteemed.
Pushing further and discussing this,
there is no other reason.
Praising those of shared nature
and denouncing those who are contrary—
this is so as to confirm the other’s wrong and make evident one’s own right;
because of shared nature with oneself,
one confirms the other’s failings and makes manifest one’s own rightness.
As for those whose order is different and mixed,
they bring no benefit to the other,
nor harm to oneself,
thus they are ordered but not esteemed.
One does not take the other as right,
nor oneself as wrong,
and there is entirely no gain or loss,
so why esteem them?
Thus, those of shared nature
often suffer from excessive praise;
for example, if both are men of strength,
the weaker admires the stronger,
and the stronger lifts up the weaker,
so their mutual praise often strays from reality.
When their fame becomes rivals,
then few can yield to one another.
If both can bear a tripod,
the desire to win arises,
and thus they cannot yield to each other.
Therefore, those who are upright in nature are fierce,
they delight in behaving uprightly toward others,
and when they see others upright,
in their hearts they appreciate them;
yet they cannot accept being reproached by others;
when their wrongs are pointed out,
they denounce the criticism and do not accept it.
Those who are forthright are emotionally exposed,
they like to act with complete honesty towards others,
and when they see others being forthright,
in their hearts they appreciate it;
yet they cannot accept the directness of others.
If someone directly points out their deficiencies,
they turn away and do not accept it.
Those who strive for reputation delight in people advancing energetically ahead of others,
and when they see someone surpassing others,
they are glad for such progress;
yet they cannot endure themselves being surpassed.
When others surpass them,
they are angry and do not submit.
Therefore, if two share the same nature but differ in ability,
they support and rely on each other;
if both have similar strength,
the stronger can encourage the weaker.
But if their natures are alike and their power is equal,
they compete and harm one another.
Fearing the other will surpass oneself,
the heart of envy arises.
This, too, is a transformation among those of shared nature,
which cannot go unexamined.
Thus there are those who support uprightness yet denounce the upright;
if another’s uprightness exceeds their own,
the heart to denounce arises.
Some associate with the wise yet denounce the wise;
if another’s wisdom surpasses their own,
then the heart of envy and harm arises.
But when most people observe these things,
they do not distinguish the underlying law;
this is the flaw of having shared nature.
If those with shared nature are already like this,
how much more those of different natures?
When a person finds themselves in a different position of power,
there exist situations of being elevated or pressed down by circumstances.
If one attains wealth and nobility,
this is the manifestation of rising power;
when one is in wealth and nobility,
nothing can subdue them.
Thus, one wears the seal of the six states,
and parents come to greet them from a hundred li away.
Poverty and humble status,
these are the manifestations of being pressed down by circumstances.
When in poverty and humble status,
how can one’s aspirations be extended and displayed?
Thus, the black sable fur coat is worn to rags,
and wives and sisters-in-law behave with disdain within the inner chambers.
As for those of highest talent,
they are able to do what others cannot do.
In all their actions, whether active or still,
these are certainly not what the masses can attain.
Therefore, the successful are labeled as hardworking and modest,
while the impoverished have well-known integrity.
When a person’s ability surpasses the average,
if they advance, they gather from the many and give to the few,
laboring and being modest to benefit the world;
if they withdraw, they tread the Way calmly,
and as recluses, remain upright and fortunate.
Those of average ability,
then, follow the gains and losses of the times.
Holding to ordinary wisdom,
their rise or fall depends on circumstance,
thus when circumstances favor, they gain;
when circumstances recede, they lose.
Therefore, relying on wealth and status, their riches fill the home,
and their generosity extends outward to others.
With surplus wealth,
they lavishly help others as they wish.
When they see one who is well-off,
they seek what is praiseworthy and speak highly of it;
moved by gratitude for favors received,
they correct that person’s wrongs;
thus, Zhū Jiàn accepted gold,
and devised strategies in return for food.
When encountering a benefactor,
they emphasize a small virtue and magnify it.
Moved by their benefactor’s support,
they promote that benefactor’s good name;
thus Cáo Qiū received hospitality,
and publicized the fame of Jì Bù.
Even without exceptional talent,
one still accomplishes things and establishes a reputation.
Is it not delightful to be wealthy and noble?
Indeed, even without good deeds, one achieves success,
even without wisdom, one establishes a name;
thus, with wealth and rank, wives and sisters-in-law show respect—
how much more so other people!
Yet in poverty and humility,
one wishes to give but has no means,
wishes to help but has no influence.
With a compassionate heart but no way to rescue others,
recognizing extraordinary talent yet unable to assist.
Relatives cannot provide relief,
and friends do not give aid.
Within, there are no offerings of vegetables for food,
without, no gifts of padded robes.
Duty and righteousness can no longer be maintained,
and affection and love gradually fall apart.
Spirit and resolve are empty and thin,
by what means can duties be upheld?
Resentment and longing both arrive,
and reproaches grow daily.
Not only do they disdain themselves,
but even words of resentment and slander arise.
Though without faults or mistakes,
still one is dismissed without reason.
Is it not fearful to be poor and lowly?
Indeed, even without cause slander arises,
and without guilt one is cast aside;
thus, in poverty and humility, wives and children are disrespectful—
how much more so other people!
Thus in the world there is extravagance and frugality,
with reputation depending on one’s advance or retreat.
Conduct is indeed up to us,
but reputation rests with the world.
Thus, a good farmer may be able to sow,
but not necessarily to reap.
If everyone under Heaven is prosperous,
then although an honest poor person suffers hardship,
he will not worry about destitution.
When families are abundant and people have enough,
even travelers along the road give to them.
Moreover, there is the high prestige of charity in words,
gaining the benefit of a glorious reputation.
Those who gain the high name of charitable speech
receive the beneficial rewards of reflected fame.
If all are poor,
then there is no one to turn to for support;
when families are impoverished and households lacking,
grain is as rare as pearls and jade,
and there is the worry of want and hardship,
and disputes of meanness and stinginess arise.
There is no one who will give when asked for help,
and sisters-in-law and uncles quarrel over husks and bran.
Thus, if one of balanced talent rises and there are those to support them,
then their character grows and they flourish;
after providing enough for themselves,
if they further dispense gifts,
then reputation is beautiful and conduct becomes established,
and all their endeavors succeed.
If private interests are low and hindered by entanglements,
and if one cannot support oneself,
then relatives are all in difficulty.
Thus one is humbled and gradually retreats.
Those above do not support,
and those below do not push forward.
Yet the observation of the masses
does not understand the root of things,
but each points to what they see,
calling those who rise “talented and able,”
and those who are pressed down as “foolish and limited.”
This is to be mistaken regarding those who are elevated or pressed down.
Though their abilities and wisdom may be equal,
noble and base take different roads;
the changes between rising and suppression
lie in wealth and poverty.
As for the refined and elegant beauty,
it reveals itself in form and substance,
and is rarely mistaken when finely observed.
Form and color display themselves outwardly,
thus they can be directly perceived.
The origins of error and confusion
always lie in two particular faults.
The birth of these two faults
sets them apart from other things.
Therefore they are not what ordinary people perceive.
Thus, the supremely subtle person
harbors essence within,
showing no adornment in outward appearance;
like gold or water shining within but not appearing bright without,
so Píng Táng, with white hair, was constrained in the position of assistant magistrate.
The supremely hollow person
boasts grand words and striking bearing,
yet is inwardly alienated and contrary.
Like a candle’s light shining outward,
but ash and cinders are dark within,
so Zhǔfù Yǎn’s eloquent speech
led to four appointments in a single year.
Yet when people seek out the extraordinary,
they cannot use subtle discernment to measure its mystery,
nor clarify the rare distinctions.
What is most peculiar and strange,
cannot be observed without true discrimination.
Some, judging by appearance, find plainness lacking,
seeing Zōng Miè’s ugly looks,
and thus suspecting him of shallowness.
Some, seeing striking bearing, regard it as greatness,
seeing Jiāng Chōng’s handsome appearance,
