and immediately calling him great.
Some take directness for mere ostentation,
and since it seems all disclosed,
doubt there is true substance.
Some take skillful embellishment as authenticity.
Eloquent words flow like a stream,
pleasing to behold.
Thus, prematurely selecting talent often leads to mistakes,
and it is better to proceed in order.
Some viewed Gān Luó as precociously accomplished,
and employed him in his youth,
but, in error, again wished to proceed in order.
Now, proceeding in order
is the common standard.
If one does not observe the reality,
where can one go and be without error?
If substance is not clearly examined,
the exceptional cannot be recognized,
thus even by proceeding in order,
one still cannot attain the right choice.
Therefore, when worthy men are passed over and worthiness brings success,
regret lies in not having been selected earlier;
thus Zhèng Bó apologized to Zhú Wǔ.
Yet when exceptional men are chosen and fail,
concern lies in not having distinguished them beforehand.
Thus Guāng Wǔ regretted it regarding Zhū Fú.
When employing one’s own wishes alone brings error,
regret lies in not having widely consulted others;
when Qín Mù disregarded Jiǎn Shū,
though he later pledged, it was too late.
When wide consultation brings harm to oneself,
the blame lies in not trusting oneself.
When Wěi Xiāo’s heart was set on Hàn,
he was led astray by Wáng Yuán.
Thus, when the colt first sets out,
all the knights may be mistaken;
when Hán Xìn established his achievements,
Huái Yīn was then shaken.
Is it that one despises the extraordinary and favors suspicion?
Rather, it is that the rarities of the world are not commonly seen,
and are remarkably unusual and beautiful.
Thus, they are not what ordinary people can recognize.
Hence, Zhāng Liáng in body was frail but in spirit mighty,
and was the outstanding one among the wise;
he was not harmed in intelligence by his slightness of form.
Jīng Shū was calm in appearance yet heroic in spirit,
and was the eminent one among the brave.
He was not hindered in valor by his mild appearance.
Therefore, those who are outstanding and eminent
are the exceptional among the multitude;
the extraordinary surpass the ordinary
and thus cannot be reached by the many.
The sage
is the most exceptional among all exceptions.
In depth of understanding, he exceeds even the most remarkable,
and thus the remarkable cannot reach him.
The more surpassing the exceptional,
the more remote their way.
Unless one possesses the utmost discernment in the land,
who could truly participate in this?
Thus, the outstanding person of one state
is a peer among his province,
but has not yet become the foremost;
what is outstanding and different among the commanderies and states,
compared to the provinces and prefectures,
also has not reached the highest rank.
The highest grade in one province
is merely a pivot among all under Heaven;
the ranks accorded by provinces and prefectures,
when compared to the outstanding of the world,
are like a pivot, yet still unattainable.
‘Pivot’
means a single turn,
it is a hinge.
The pivots of the world
have relative degrees—some superior, some inferior.
Heroic men are not passed down from age to age,
thus Yī, Lǚ, Guǎn, and Yàn
emerged precisely as circumstances required.
Hence what the masses value
is always what is outstanding relative to themselves;
if talent and wisdom surpass them,
they deem it valuable,
though they do not value what is most exceptional.
What is most exceptional
is not recognized by ordinary people.
Thus the clear-sighted among the people
can only know the tally of their contemporaries;
those with greater discernment
barely recognize the outstanding ones from states and commanderies.
Yet they cannot understand the proportions of the highest grades;
much less discern the foremost outstanding ones of a state or commandery.
The clear-sighted among the peers
can understand the scale of the foremost grades;
those most distinguished among their peers
may barely recognize the finest of the top-ranking men in the commanderies.
Yet they cannot recognize those of the utmost exception;
nor comprehend the principles behind what makes them uniquely strange.
Only those who are supremely exceptional
can know the teachings of the sage;
seeing it before them,
and in a flash, it is behind.
Yet they cannot fully reach the innermost mysteries.
If there were one who stood in lofty distinction,
though others wished to emulate him,
it would not be possible.
Thus to conclude,
the principles of human character and talent
are wondrous and cannot be completely fathomed.
All we can do is attempt to describe them in form,
analogizing to what things are apt,
observing how they connect and flow together,
and merely raising a corner of the whole.
On the Difficulty of Recommending the Worthy, Chapter Eleven
Human talents are subtle and profound;
indeed, they are difficult to know.
To accurately discern them is hard;
to recommend them effectively is even harder.
“Imitating Difficulty,” Chapter Eleven
It is generally held that there are two difficulties in assessing people:
there is the difficulty of discerning what is hard to know,
especially when their conduct is extraordinary and diverse,
making them hard to comprehend.
There is also the difficulty of acting upon knowledge without means to realize its benefit.
Though you may understand a person,
you may have no way to recommend them.
What is meant by the difficulty of discerning what is hard to know?
The character of individuals is subtle,
intelligence has no form or shape,
and the extraordinary are rare and exquisite.
They are capable of spiritual clarity,
and though one wishes to enter into their spirit
and clarify their intelligence,
the path is exceedingly hard,
and so it is indeed the difficulty of discerning what is hard to know.
To know people is wisdom;
only the Emperor finds it truly difficult—
how much more so for ordinary people!
Therefore, among the masses, discernment cannot be entirely sufficient:
each keeps to his own perspective.
Thus each establishes his own standard
and observes others accordingly.
Using one's own abilities,
one makes a survey of various talents.
Sometimes they assess a person's appearance,
judging talent by outward form.
Sometimes they observe movements,
evaluating merit by conduct and progress.
Sometimes they weigh beginnings and ends,
seeking the upright in others.
Sometimes they compare similarities,
seeking meaning through intention.
Sometimes they infer from minute details,
judging by emotion and reason.
Sometimes out of fear of faults and errors,
they judge with simplicity and forgiveness.
Sometimes they follow what people say,
taking words as a measure.
Sometimes they examine actions,
judging people by their achievements and efficiency.
These eight methods intermingle,
each taking personal preference as the standard,
which results in confusion and lack of order.
Hence those who are rightly recognized are few,
and those who are missed are many.
Only what is similar to oneself is selected,
so what differs from oneself is lost.
One cannot encompass everything,
and thus what is missed is many.
For this reason, errors often arise from forming judgments based on superficial likeness,
when selection by appearance leads actions astray.
There is also the folly of judging by one's place or circumstances:
one may be physically in Jiānghǎi,
yet one's heart remains with Wèi Què.
Thus, when encountering and judging people,
one follows reputation and hearsay,
and fails to grasp their true nature.
That is why sages listen to words and observe deeds:
if there is praise,
there must be a test.
Thus, superficial excellence displayed openly
is taken as something extraordinary;
intelligence that is shallow and easy to perceive
appears as rare talent.
Deep insight, kept hidden and silent,
is deemed empty or void;
intelligence that is profound and inwardly luminous
appears as lacking substance.
Distinguishing subtle truths
is taken for Lílóu;
investigating the ultimate principle with utmost precision
appears to be the same as Lílóu.
Reciting grades and ranks orally
is accepted as doctrine and principle;
forcibly categorizing things
seems to suggest reason.
To enjoy speaking of rights and wrongs
is taken to be judgment of good and bad;
to recklessly argue right and wrong
seems to clarify virtue and vice.
Assigning names and categories in discourse
is taken as knowing people;
forcibly discussing the worthy and the unworthy
seems to demonstrate insight into character.
Discussing government in a neutral manner
is deemed to display an understanding of the state;
recklessly debating current affairs
seems to show understanding of the nation’s condition.
It is like listening to different sounds:
names are given to things according to their sounds.
If these seven cannot be distinguished,
things are always named by mere appearances,
like hearing the sound of a cat and calling it a cat,
or the sound of a sparrow and calling it a sparrow,
without knowing what these creatures are actually called.
The confusion and doubt of the world
all arise from such cases.
Thus, in the State of Lǔ, those who wore Confucian robes
were all called Confucians,
but if you stood up and questioned them,
there would be but one true Confucian among them.
Mere name without substance,
proves useless in application:
the Southern Sieve cannot be used for winnowing;
the Běidǒu cannot be dipped for wine.
Thus it is said:
a name comes from the mouth,
but substance is lost in practice.
The masses see only appearance and assign names,
so use proves inauthentic.
Those with true substance within,
find name and reality do not coincide;
but with use comes effectiveness,
for true wisdom resides within,
which the masses cannot see.
Thus there is no outward name, but there is inner substance.
Therefore, as the multitude withdraws a name,
substance is revealed by real deeds;
when ability is established, a name becomes manifest.
This is the common error in superficial judgment.
Shallow intelligence lacks completion;
deep intelligence has no obvious beginning.
So when the masses attempt to judge,
they often fail from the outset.
It is only after dwelling with someone
that you come to know them.
You watch where they settle,
observe where they reside,
yet might still not understand.
Therefore, in assessing where they dwell:
observe where they find comfort;
those who hold to old habits
are sincere in benevolence.
In those of influence,
observe what they promote;
those who promote uprightness
are devoted to righteousness.
In the wealthy,
observe to whom they give;
those who give to the upright and robust
are clear in propriety.
In the impoverished,
observe what they do;
those who persist in learning and the classics
are diligent in wisdom.
In the poor,
observe what they seek;
those who seek what is due to them
are true to faith.
Only in this way can one truly discern the worthy and unworthy.
Those who do so are the worthy;
those who do otherwise are not.
Yet even this requires testing,
and is not the beginning of recognition.
If it is only through testing that one knows,
can that still be called recognition?
This is enough to understand someone’s quality,
but not enough to know their resourcefulness.
Resourcefulness lies in adaptability,
and cannot be judged according to fixed standards.
Moreover, the people of the world,
cannot all be engaged with personally.
Therefore, by observing their outward conduct,
you may know one part,
but cannot know the whole.
Some change their aspirations and interests,
adapting themselves according to circumstance;
thus Shìzǔ erred in judging Páng Méng,
and Cáo Gōng erred in judging Dǒng Zhuó.
Some show longing before arriving,
some change attitudes after arriving;
Lǐ Yì was at first wholly devoted to Guāng Wǔ,
but in the end transferred his loyalty to Shèng Gōng.
Some persist under hardship,
others indulge their desires once in power.
Wáng Mǎng at first wore plain clothing and practiced humility,
but ended in extreme extravagance and luxury.
This again shows the error of judging by dwelling and circumstances.
Human feelings are so variable—
who can fix them?
From this it can be inferred
that to grasp both the essence and the adaptation
is the very difficulty of discerning what is hard to know.
Once you know their disposition
and investigate their changes,
it is beyond the capacity of ordinary people to judge.
What is meant by the difficulty of having no means to achieve one's usefulness?
Those of outstanding talent are often not recognized,
and are difficult to discern and know.
Sometimes those recognized are among the young and humble,
but before they make their way, they meet an early end;
before they can advance,
the person has already died.
Sometimes, those recognized
are not yet elevated before passing away;
before they can be selected and promoted,
they have already left this world.
Sometimes, when the tune is lofty, few can harmonize with it,
and a singer receives no praise;
Gōngshū Zuò recommended Shāng Yāng,
but the Wèi Wáng could not employ him.
Sometimes, one is of low station and feeble strength,
and one's words are not appreciated;
Qín Xī recommended Bǎilǐ Xī,
but both head and feet were crushed.
Sometimes, one's skills are not in favor with the times,
and are not trusted or esteemed;
Empress Dòu favored the teachings of Huáng-Lǎo,
so how could Confucian scholars hope to advance?
Sometimes, one is not in the right position,
and has no way to be selected;
Biàn Hé, because he was not among craftsmen,
had to carry the uncut jade and weep.
Sometimes, one holds the right position,
yet is constrained or oppressed.
Hé Wǔ nominated Gōngsūn Lù,
but he was pushed aside by the Wáng clan.
Thus, for true talent to be recognized,
it is a chance of one in ten thousand.
Even if one's abilities are excellent,
one must meet a kindred spirit.
Even if a kindred spirit is found,
one must encounter an enlightened ruler.
The meeting of all three,
is rarer than one in ten thousand.
To have true recognition in office,
truly occurs less than one in a hundred cases.
Even if one knows one's true worth,
sometimes one is not in office.
If, according to position and opportunity, one can be recommended and appointed,
this should happen less than once in ten times.
Recognition requires being in office,
and insightful attainment further requires suitability.
Sometimes, even with the wisdom to recognize true worth,
there is some hindrance or deprivation,
and one does not wish to put forward a recommendation;
thus, though able to distinguish the worthy from the unworthy, one is constrained by hindrance and deprivation,
and so is unwilling.
Sometimes there is a love of recommending talent,
but not the ability to recognize the true ones.
Among those in office,
though their hearts are inclined to the worthy and good,
their discernment is insufficient to recognize them.
Therefore, knowledge and ignorance
mix chaotically among the masses.
Sometimes, a person loves the worthy but does not recognize them,
or, knowing the worthy, harbors jealousy,
so that use and nonuse
are all mixed with the general multitude,
tangled and confused.
Those who truly know
suffer from not being able to put their abilities to use;
without rank or place,
they have no way to make themselves effective.
Those who do not know,
likewise believe themselves unacquainted.
Even if they hold office,
they cannot recognize talent.
This is the so-called difficulty of having no means to achieve one’s usefulness.
Therefore, it is said that there are two difficulties in utilizing men.
Thus, the ruler should always employ his intelligence and wisdom,
broaden his vision and hearing,
shed light on what is hidden and obscure,
widely seek outstanding and able people,
promote the capable without avoiding enemies,
raise the worthy without neglecting those hidden in obscurity,
and only then can the state be well governed,
and achievements successfully accomplished.
Discourse on Quelling Disputes, Chapter Twelve
The virtuous and good do not boast,
much less over trifles.
Letting go of resentment and ceasing to quarrel,
one will surely attain honor and fortune.
"Explaining Disputes," Chapter Twelve
In general, excelling without boasting is greatness;
to do good and boast of one’s own abilities
is what the masses consider petty.
To be worthy and yet pride oneself brings loss.
Practice virtue and remove the thought of self-importance,
and wherever you go, how can it not be to your benefit!
Thus, Shùn yielded to virtue,
and his righteousness became renowned;
Tāng humbled himself without hesitation,
and each day his sageliness and reverence grew.
Although these two Emperors were endowed by Heaven with sagely virtue,
born as the highest sages,
they still cherished labor and humility,
were quick to act in stepping back and yielding,
whereupon their trustworthiness and righteousness became well known,
and they gloriously occupied the throne of Heaven.
Qì reached the heights of humanity,
yet became ever more oppressive toward those below;
Wáng Shū delighted in contention,
and in the end, he fled in exile.
These two great ministers boasted of their achievements and looked down on others,
one saw his clan utterly destroyed,
the other escaped calamity in flight.
From this it can be seen:
the way of contention and yielding—
is it not clearly set apart!
Thus, the one who is humble and yields,
follows the flourishing path to advancement;
the reason the rivers and seas are king of the hundred valleys
is because they dwell in lowliness.
To boast and strive arrogantly,
is to walk the perilous road to ruin;
the reason the rhinoceros and tiger crash against their cages
is because their natures are fierce and biting.
Therefore, the gentleman in all actions dares not transgress the standards of ritual;
his resolve dares not overstep the proper tracks.
His feet do not tread recklessly,
he always cherishes retreat and yielding.
Inwardly, he works hard to help himself;
outwardly, he is modest and yielding, acting respectfully and with fear.
Alone, he dares not do what is wrong;
when he leaves his door, he behaves as if meeting a great guest.
Thus, resentment and trouble do not befall him,
and honor and blessings endure long.
External things cannot harm him,
and his descendants rely on this to avoid calamity.
But the petty man is not so:
he boasts of achievements and flaunts his talents,
delighting in overwhelming others.
From the start, whether great or small,
his heart soars arrogantly to dominate others.
Thus, those in the forefront are harmed by others;
if one flaunts skill and acts unrestrained,
it is human nature to harm him.
If one achieves merit, people destroy him;
if proud and overflowing because of merit,
it is human nature to bring him down.
Those who are ruined and defeated, others rejoice in it.
When they finally fall and perish,
it is what others enjoy seeing.
Thus, when driving side by side racing to get ahead,
yet unable to take anything from each other,
petty men compete to advance,
but their wisdom is equal;
racing together on a dangerous path,
they trample over one another.
Both collapse,
and are overtaken by those behind.
They die halfway down the road,
and those behind seize their place;
like a rabbit slain and a dog worn out,
the farmer reaps the reward.
From this reasoning,
the routes of contention and yielding—
their difference is clear indeed.
The gentleman esteems yielding,
so even traveling ten thousand li his road remains clear;
the petty man delights in contention,
and before even taking a step, his path is blocked.
However, those who are fond of competing for superiority
still claim this is not so.
The greedy are fond of vying for superiority;
even if they hear of the virtuous custom of yielding,
their minds remain clouded.
Thus they say that the ancients gained by yielding,
but that people today lose by yielding.
Whatever their hearts approve,
they rise and contend for it.
They regard being in front as swift and sharp,
while being behind is seen as slow and stagnant;
therefore, whether walking or sitting, they are restless with anxiety,
having no time to oil their carts.
They see being below the multitude as humble and constrained,
but stepping on others as exceptional and outstanding;
if one can boast of surpassing others,
one does not feel shame even when riding another’s carriage.
They take yielding to an adversary as turning towards humiliation,
and overstepping superiors as lofty and impressive.
Thus Zhào Chuān showed no regard for the general,
and Zhìzǐ led his smaller forces to destruction.
For this reason, when boldly striving ahead,
they cannot reflect upon themselves.
It is like tigers and wolves eating living creatures,
coming to possess murderous fury against humans.
If one is haughty before the worthy,
he will certainly encounter humility and deference;
Xiàng Rú yielded to Lián Pō,
and so both obtained benefit.
If one is haughty before the violent,
enmity and hardship will inevitably arise.
Guàn Fū would not bow to Tián Fén,
so both suffered greatly.
Once enmity and hardship have arisen,
then right and wrong become mixed and hard to clarify;
each justifies himself and condemns the other,
who can discern the truth?
When confusion makes matters hard to clarify,
how is this different from self-destruction?
When two tigers fight,
the smaller dies,
the larger is wounded,
how can both remain intact?
Moreover, when people harm themselves,
it all springs from resentment and offense, which develops into disaster;
if there were originally no resentment or hatred,
and only circumstantial encounters,
it would not result in harm.
It is always by relying on affairs,
and embellishing them at the start or end.
Whenever people slander and defame,
it is always by taking incidents and ornamenting them.
As for the listeners,
even if they do not fully believe,
still, half consider it so.
Because in speech there is a point of departure,
so half believe it.
Retaliation by oneself
is likewise the same.
One repays slander in return,
causing it to grow wings and a tail.
In the end,
both sides receive half.
Trust becomes established both near and far.
Both have visible forms,
though the truth is unknown.
Thus, whether listeners are near or far,
half believe this side,
half believe that side.
If so, those who have impetuous tempers and argue fiercely
end up sparring with words and harming themselves;
if one speaks of another’s faults,
others will also speak of his own filth;
even when reviling others,
he only invites revilement upon himself.
Those who compete in speech and debate,
are but lending their hands to beat themselves.
If words are spoken angrily, strength compels contention;
when one strikes others,
others strike back,
this is lending a hand to beat oneself.
How could such deluded confusion not be extreme!
Lending a hand to beat oneself,
lending a mouth to revile oneself,
what is this if not delusion?
If we trace the origin,
is there anyone who, thoroughly examining himself,
comes to cause recrimination and lawsuits?
If one can reproach oneself,
others will likewise reproach themselves;
if neither speaks in rivalry,
how can contention and litigation arise?
It all stems from insufficient tolerance within,
and endless expectations placed outwardly.
Thus, the reason for contention
is inner inability to tolerate and blame oneself,
while outwardly, endless expectation of others.
Either resenting others for slighting oneself,
or hating others for surpassing oneself.
So as the mind battles,
there will never be rest.
If I am shallow and others slight me,
then it is because I am at fault and they are in the right;
to be wrong and yet be slighted
is only natural.
If I am virtuous and others do not recognize it,
then being slighted is not my blame.
If intimacy brings harm,
this too is only natural.
If others are virtuous and stand before me,
then my own virtue has not yet reached theirs;
that their virtue is lighter falls on them,
which is also as it should be.
If our virtues are equal and they come before me,
then my virtue is next in line.
Equal virtue and difference in age,
that is as it commonly is.
What is there to resent?
Moreover, if two worthy people are not distinguished,
then the one who can yield is outstanding;
if their talents are equal and they do not vie for superiority,
the multitude praises their yielding.
But if the outstanding are not distinguished,
then the one who exerts himself becomes exhausted.
If the worthy are equal and reputation is not distinguished,
the multitude despises their fighting.
Therefore Lìn Xiàng Rú decided victory over Lián Pō by turning his carriage around,
Kòu Xún gained honor over Jiǎ Fù by refusing to fight.
These two worthy men,
knowing the path of contention could not be followed,
thus turned their carriages to retreat or welcomed each other with wine and roasted meat;
thus both Lián and Jiǎ bared their arms in apology,
and the rivalry was resolved.
When the trend of things reverses,
this is what the gentleman calls the Way.
The dragon and the snake withdraw to preserve their lives,
the inchworm contracts in order to extend itself.
Among insects and small creatures,
they still know how to bend and coil;
how much more so with people!
Therefore, the junzǐ knows that to yield is to be able to extend oneself,
so he endures humiliation without complaint;
Hán Xìn endured the humiliation of crawling between someone’s legs.
He understands that humility and deference enable victory over enemies,
so he lowers himself without doubt.
This is what is meant by Zhǎn Xǐ feasting the Qí army.
When matters reach their extreme,
misfortune is thereby turned into good fortune;
Jìn Wén avoided Chǔ by three stations,
and thus achieved merit at Chéngpú.
By humbling enemies, he turns them into friends;
he treated Lián Pō as his superior,
and became a friend willing to die together.
Thus, resentment and enmity do not linger to the descendants,
and a good name is spread infinitely.
The sons and grandsons inherit the glory and protection,
and their noble deeds are recorded on bamboo and silk.
Is not this the way of the junzǐ
abundant indeed?
If one is partial, anxious, and likes to contend,
then he will bring danger upon himself in his own time;
how could those who come later attain good fortune?
Moreover, the junzǐ is able to endure minor slights,
so there are no great lawsuits arising from quarrels;
great lawsuits begin from little incidents,
therefore the junzǐ is careful about small matters.
The xiǎorén cannot endure small angers,
and ends up suffering enormous humiliations and defeats.
The xiǎorén considers small evils to be harmless and does not remove them,
so the crimes grow large and cannot be resolved,
evil accumulates and cannot be saved.
If resentment is slight and one yields to it,
it may still be called humble virtue;
when resentment is subtle,
humble virtue can remove it.
If trouble is incipient and one contends,
then disaster will be complete and cannot be averted.
A trickle that does not cease
eventually forms rivers and streams;
if water leaks and overturns a boat,
how can it be rescued?
Therefore, Chén Yú because of the quarrel with Zhāng Ěr,
in the end suffered the harm of separation and death;
hoping for a moment’s revenge,
he forgot a lifetime’s evil,
thus destroyed himself and cut off his line.
Péng Chǒng, because of the rift with Zhū Fú,
in the end suffered the calamity of total destruction.
Resenting a small instance of reprimand,
he contravened the great plan for the beginning and end;
therefore his clan was cut off and his family reduced.
The turning point between disaster and fortune—
how could one not be cautious!
Two women quarreled over mulberry leaves,
and thus the conflict between Wú and Chǔ began;
Jì Hòu fought over chickens,
and trouble for the state of Lǔ arose.
How could one not be fearful!
How could one not be fearful!
Therefore, when the jūnzǐ seeks victory,
he takes yielding as his sharpest advantage;
wherever yielding reaches,
before him no enemy can withstand.
He uses cultivating himself as his shield and tower,
and perfects himself with reverence,
so that nothing can harm him.
When still, he closes the mysterious gate with silence;
when active, he follows the open road of humility and obedience.
If the time allows stillness,
he redoubles his closure and deepens his silence;
if the time allows action,
he treads the path of righteousness and then advances.
Thus, when he conquers in conflict, his contention is not made manifest;
harmonizing activity and stillness at the proper measure,
he attains victory with no one opposing him;
his contest is not by force,
and so his success is plainly seen.
The enemy submits but bears no resentment.
Weapons are not used,
so how could resentment arise?
For him, regret or greedy desire do not manifest in outward display;
how could there be any overt contention?
Even his expression remains unmoved,
how much less would he strive in forceful struggle?
Those who contend openly,
must be those who consider themselves worthy,
yet others see them as devious and twisted.
Considering oneself worthy,
standing firm in self-righteousness,
is to value oneself and belittle others;
can others not contend in return?
If one truly lacks base character,
then there is nothing for others to reproach;
if indeed there is base character,
then who could contest with such a person?
To contend with one who is devious,
is like caging an aurochs and provoking a tiger—
can that end well?
In anger, one harms others,
that is inevitable.
The Yìjīng says:
"To be devious and act in contrary ways,
this is litigation."
"Contention will surely draw forth a multitude."
That is, to harbor deviousness and act contrarily,
must lead to stirring up crowds and resulting in litigation.
Lǎozǐ says:
"Because he alone does not contend,
therefore in all under Heaven none can contest with him."
One who values humility and yielding
meets with no contention wherever he goes.
Therefore, the jūnzǐ knows the path of contention cannot be followed.
To tread the path of conflict,
will surely lead to overturned chariots and disaster.
Therefore, the customs of Yuè ascend to the heights,
walking alone above the three ranks.
What are the three ranks?
To be without merit yet boast of oneself,
is the first rank;
to be empty and boastful,
is thus the lowest rank.
To have merit and flaunt it,
is the second rank;
to vaunt one's own abilities,
is thus the middle rank.
To have great merit and not flaunt it,
is the third rank.
To attribute achievement to others,
is thus the highest rank.
To be foolish yet eager to win,
is the first rank;
to be unaware of one’s own measure,
is thus the lowest rank.
To be virtuous but esteem others,
is the second rank;
to admire one's own abilities,
is thus the middle rank.
To be virtuous and able to yield,
is the third rank.
To ascribe goodness to others,
is thus the highest rank.
To delay oneself and hasten to aid others,
is the first rank;
to be by nature without forgiveness toward others,
is thus the lowest rank.
To hasten for oneself and others alike,
is the second rank;
to be narrow and harsh,
is thus the middle rank.
To hasten for oneself yet be lenient to others,
is the third rank.
To be cautious in conduct and forgiving toward others,
is thus the highest rank.
All these several cases,
are the marvelous workings of the Dào,
the transformations of things.
When the mind is not simple and unified,
this is being strange and variable.
Only after three transformations is it attained,
thus none can reach it.
The petty person dwells content in the lowest rank,
how could he ever attain it!
Only those who know the Dào and comprehend transformation,
can thus abide in it.
Such ones dwell in the highest rank and do not lose it.
Therefore, Mèngzhī Fǎn, by not boasting,
gained the praise of the sages;
not boasting of his achievements,
noble reputation arose of itself.
Guǎn Shū, by declining reward,
received a gift of honor and esteem.
Not coveting reward,
he gained honor naturally.
Was this gained by seeking opportunities through cunning?
Rather, it was the spontaneous union of pure virtue and nature.
Was it intentionally not boasting, declining reward, or seeking glory through crooked intent?
Instead, it simply flowed straight from within,
uniting itself with principle.
Such a gentleman knows that self-diminution is a gain,
thus achieving one deed but gaining twice the praise;
diminishing oneself, actions are accomplished and fame established.
The petty person does not know that self-benefit is a loss,
so by one boast loses all.
Boasting brings about ruin and loss of reputation.
Judging from this,
not boasting
is truly boasting;
not contending
is truly contending.
Without boasting and reputation is manifest,
without contending and principle is attained.
Yielding to one's opponent,
is to conquer him;
placing oneself below the crowd,
is to rise above them.
By retreated yielding, the opponent submits;
with humble honor, virtue shines forth.
If the gentleman can truly see the perilous reputation on the path of contention,
and ride alone to the height of the mysterious way,
then his radiance will shine brilliantly and daily renew itself,
and his virtue and voice will be ranked among the ancients.
By avoiding the dangerous road of unbridled anger,
and wandering alone in the highest rank,
remaining far from the chattering sparrows,
and in solitary harmony with the cry of the phoenix in the vast and mysterious,
then his virtue and brilliance will shine on future generations,
and his pure light will rival the ages past.
